articles.title: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic opportunity, economic imperative or geopolitical gamble? - MyJoyOnline
articles.summary: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic opportunity, economic imperative or geopolitical gamble?  MyJoyOnline
articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
Walk through Abossey Okai, Tema and other industrial enclaves in Ghana and you can already see BRICS in Ghana's economy: spare parts and machinery from Guangzhou, pharmaceuticals and vehicles from India, gold flowing out to Dubai.
Samuel Okudzeto Abalakwa, Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister, announced cabinet’s approval for Ghana’s application to join the BRICS, at a joint press briefing with India’s External Affairs Minister during his visit to Accra. The Honourable Minister linked the decision to the President’s “New Economy” agenda and the desire for Ghana to chart its own path without being constrained by the conditionalities of a few international institutions. This announcement formalises a relationship that trade data has been describing for years.
The open questions are what formal membership adds, what it might cost, and how businesses should position themselves while the process plays out. The conversation is more relevant now, as Ghana transitions from a period of macroeconomic stabilisation towards one focused on investment-led growth and structural transformation.
Understanding BRICS and Why It Matters
What began in the early 2000s as an economic acronym coined to describe the fast-growing emerging economies of Brazil, Russia, India and China has evolved into one of the most influential geopolitical and economic blocs in the world. South Africa joined the grouping in 2010, transforming BRIC into BRICS and providing Africa with representation within the bloc. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE later joined, followed by Indonesia in 2025, bringing membership to 11, with Nigeria and several other countries holding partner status.
The group’s main institution is the New Development Bank (NDB), headquartered in Shanghai. The bank has approved over 120 projects worth about US$40 billion and admits new members on the condition that the founding BRICS countries' capital share never falls below 55%. One stated ambition - reducing reliance on the US Dollar - remains a key aspiration yet to be realised.
BRICS today is no longer simply a forum for emerging economies. It represents a broader vision for increasing the influence of developing nations within global governance structures. For many countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America, the appeal of BRICS lies not in replacing existing global institutions, but in creating additional options. In an increasingly uncertain global environment characterised by economic fragmentation, geopolitical competition and shifting trade dynamics, diversification has become a strategic necessity.
Why Ghana Is Looking Towards BRICS
Ghana's interest in BRICS comes at a pivotal moment in its economic journey.
Following years of economic turbulence, debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms, the Country has made notable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability. Economic discussions are increasingly shifting from stabilisation towards growth, productivity, investment and industrialisation. Internal economic briefings and policy discussions increasingly focus on how Ghana can move from recovery to sustainable private-sector-led growth.
At the same time, the global economic environment is changing. Emerging markets are playing a larger role in global trade and investment flows, while developing countries are seeking greater influence within international institutions.
Against this backdrop, BRICS presents Ghana with an opportunity to expand its economic options.
Government officials have publicly framed the proposed membership as part of a broader strategy to diversify international partnerships and create new avenues for cooperation. This rationale aligns closely with the Country's broader ambitions around industrialisation, infrastructure development, job creation and economic transformation.
The Economic Case for Membership
The strongest arguments in favour of Ghana joining BRICS are arguably economic rather than political. Four key areas of potential benefit to Ghana have been highlighted below:
- Alignment with where Ghana's trade already goes: This is the strongest economic argument. In 2025, the UAE took 25.9% of Ghana's exports, India 16.0%, South Africa 10.3% and China 4.9%. All four are BRICS members, which means roughly 57% of Ghana's export earnings already flow to the bloc. On the import side, China remained Ghana's largest supplier at about 23% of imports in the fourth quarter of 2025. Membership could institutionalise relationships that are already central to Ghana's balance of payments, while opening additional channels for exports and investment promotion.
- Development financing options: Ghana has completed a demanding IMF programme and now engages the Fund through a Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI), a non-financing arrangement that offers technical support and policy guidance. With no IMF money on the table, access to the NDB for infrastructure financing (energy, rail, water, digital) would widen the menu of long-tenor capital at a time when Ghana needs to finance growth. These investments will be essential if the Country is to realise its ambition of becoming a competitive industrial economy.
- Industrial and technology partnerships: The visit by India’s External Affairs Minister itself showed what is on offer, with plans announced to deepen cooperation in railways, pharmaceuticals, ICT, defence, agriculture and science and technology. If Ghana uses membership to negotiate local value addition, such as gold refining, cocoa processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing, rather than simply more raw commodity exports, the growth dividend could be real.
- Negotiating leverage: Being in more rooms strengthens Ghana's hand with every partner, including the Bretton Woods institutions, on debt treatment, climate finance and conditionality, amongst others.
Lessons from Africa's BRICS Experience
To understand what BRICS membership could mean for Ghana, it is important to examine the experiences of African countries already within the bloc.
South Africa's journey offers perhaps the most relevant case study. Since joining BRICS in 2010, South Africa has used the platform to deepen trade and investment relationships, expand diplomatic influence and access development financing through the New Development Bank. The NDB's first South African loan in 2016 supported renewable energy, and the bank has since backed 13 projects there worth around US$9 billion (in current terms), including a loan of up to US$1 billion for water and sanitation infrastructure under the Municipal Infrastructure Grant programme. The lesson is that the NDB can be a meaningful infrastructure financier for a member with a strong project pipeline and capable state entities. The Country continues to benefit from this association, while simultaneously maintaining strong economic relationships with Europe and the United States.
Ethiopia, which joined in 2024, presents a cautionary story. At admission, one Ethiopian economist judged that the direct economic benefit would be modest, but that membership would improve investor perception and widen options for development finance. Ethiopian analysts have observed that the country's trade and investment ties are stronger with individual BRICS countries such as China, Saudi Arabia and India than with the bloc as a whole, and that membership has not offset the AGOA benefits and Western privileges that were lost. The Ethiopian Economics Association also warned that trading in local currencies could worsen forex constraints and complicate Dollar-based trade with other partners, recommending that Ethiopia manages it relationship with both BRICS and the West in the short run to the benefit of the country.
Perhaps the most important lesson from these experiences is that BRICS membership itself does not create economic transformation. Membership rewards countries that come with bankable projects and strong institutions, and it does not by itself replace Western market access. South Africa's gains did not emerge simply because it joined BRICS; they emerged because the country actively leveraged membership to attract investment, strengthen trade relationships and promote national economic priorities.
The challenges and considerations
While the economic opportunities are compelling, it would be naïve to assume that BRICS membership comes without risks.
- Western Economic Relationships management is an immediate risk: The European Union, United States and United Kingdom remain among Ghana's most important development partners, export destinations and sources of foreign direct investment. President Trump has threatened additional tariffs on countries that align with what he describes as the bloc's anti-American policies. Even though Ghana’s bilateral goods trade with the US is not relatively huge, it matters disproportionately for specific sectors. With AGOA renewal and trade negotiations unsettled, the timing requires careful diplomacy. Ghana's engagement with BRICS should not be interpreted as a pivot away from the West. Such a framing creates a false choice. The world's most successful middle-income economies typically pursue diversified international relationships rather than exclusive alliances. The strategic objective should be to broaden Ghana's options, not narrow them.
- Trade imbalance and import competition: Concerns have been raised on whether Ghana, as a largely import-driven economy, risks becoming a dumping ground for larger BRICS producers such as China. Trade defence and local-content policies must be reviewed to ensure Ghanaian manufacturers are not squeezed in the pursuit of deeper integration.
- Choice of membership tier: The membership option being considered is of significant strategic importance. The UK government has formally introduced a revised national planning policy for port development, replacing the framework that has governed major port infrastructure projects since 2012.
The updated National Policy Statement for Ports came into force on October 15 following parliamentary scrutiny.
It establishes the policy framework used to assess nationally significant port infrastructure proposals, including major terminal developments and associated road and rail connections.
The policy applies to ports in England and to reserved trust ports in Wales, currently Milford Haven.
The government says the revised framework is designed to support private investment in port infrastructure while addressing changing market requirements, national resilience and environmental considerations.
The Department for Transport presented the revised policy to Parliament in July. It has now taken effect after the statutory 21-sitting-day scrutiny period passed without a resolution opposing the changes.

articles.full_text:
Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay on Wednesday hit out at Donald Trump's "illegal" sanctions against the International Criminal Court, saying the US president needed a lesson in international law.
In an interview with AFP, Pillay also said it was no coincidence the US sanctions on the ICC were announced just hours after her Nobel, as a "reaction to the fact that the award was not given to President Trump."
Asked what her message was for Trump, the 85-year-old judge told AFP: "Call in your legal advisors to explain to you what international law is."
"He should call in his advisors to tell him why we say that it is unlawful for him to interfere with an independent international court."
On Friday, the US announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick-by-brick", furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
Pillay noted that previous US administrations had welcomed an ICC arrest warrant against Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying, "that's selective, that's double standards, and that's wrong."
The sanctions, which will hit the court's technology and banking operations, take effect in six months and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has urged talks with Washington during that time to discuss reforms to the court, based in The Hague.
But Pillay said the idea of reforms to the ICC was "euphemistic", adding that what Trump wanted was "an undertaking that they won't pursue investigations of US citizens."
"You can't do that, because you can't have double standards. You can't selectively pursue one lot of people and not the other," Pillay told AFP.
"It will be such a bad, dangerous precedent."
- 'Hurtful and insulting' -
Pillay also hit back at Israeli officials who reacted with outrage to her Nobel, after she headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which found last year that genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Netanyahu called her a "bigot" while Israel's foreign ministry said Nazi propagandist Joseph Goebbels must be "applauding from hell" at her award.
"I think it's very hurtful and insulting," said Pillay.
"Goebbels had blood on his hands....responsible for the death of thousands of people. Not only Jews, but people of colour like me," she added.
She acknowledged there was little political appetite to arrest Netanyahu to face the ICC accusations, which he furiously denies.
"But all my life I've seen people get around difficulties, so I'm confident that it will happen," she said, asked if Netanyahu was ever likely to appear in the ICC dock.
- 'Age will constrain me' -
Pillay said she was still digesting the news that she had won. She found it difficult to believe at first "because they give their awards to very few women -- gross inequality in the practice so far."
At 85, she frets she will be unable to travel far and wide to sing the praises of international justice with the amplified voice of a Nobel Peace Prize winner.
"I think that age will constrain me somewhat. I can't be as active as I used to," she said, noting that she visited 79 countries when she was UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
She said she was consulting people about how best to spend the 12 million Swedish krone prize ($1.2 million) but hinted some of it might be invested in her native South Africa.
"Africa is suffering. South Africa is suffering. It's very difficult to raise funds there," she said.
"The University of KwaZulu-Natal has set up a unit in my name, so I'll begin to have discussions with them. I believe in education for children and the youth."
AFP

By Ajong Mbapndah L
Mozambique’s ambitions to become a leading maritime and logistics hub in Southern Africa have received a major boost with the launch of a US$150 million dredging project at the Port of Maputo, backed by the Maputo Port Development Company (MPDC) and its partner, global logistics giant DP World.
The investment, formally launched on October 12, 2026, at a ceremony attended by Mozambican President Daniel Francisco Chapo and Minister of Transport and Logistics João Jorge Matlombe, marks another milestone in the modernization of one of Southern Africa’s most important maritime gateways. The project will deepen and widen the port’s access channel, allowing larger vessels to dock while improving shipping efficiency and strengthening Mozambique’s competitiveness in regional and international trade.
Mohammed Akoojee, CEO and Managing Director for Africa at DP World, welcomed the development, describing it as an important milestone in the company’s partnership with MPDC and its commitment to expanding trade opportunities across the region.
“Together with DP World’s increased investments in the development of the container terminal at the Port of Maputo, this project is designed to strengthen the port’s competitiveness and expand Southern Africa’s access to international markets,” Akoojee stated in a message shared on LinkedIn.
The announcement comes as African countries intensify efforts to modernize transport infrastructure, reduce logistics costs and improve connectivity between production centers, regional markets and global shipping networks.
$150 Million Investment to Accommodate Larger Vessels
The capital dredging project will deepen the Port of Maputo’s access channel to 15.3 metres and widen its straight sections from 110 metres to 210 metres, enabling the port to accommodate vessels measuring up to 366 metres in length.
The ambitious engineering operation, expected to take approximately 12 months, will involve the removal of an estimated 21.2 million cubic metres of material using seven specialized vessels.
Once completed, the improvements are expected to enhance maritime access, reduce navigational constraints and strengthen the port’s ability to handle larger commercial vessels serving regional and international markets.
For Mozambique, the investment carries significance beyond the port itself. Maputo occupies a strategic position along the southern African coastline, providing access to important industrial, agricultural and mining markets in neighboring countries, particularly South Africa and Eswatini.
The port also serves as an important outlet for cargo moving through regional transport corridors, making its continued development central to Southern Africa’s broader economic integration and trade expansion.
By improving access for larger ships, the project could help shipping companies achieve greater economies of scale while providing regional exporters with more competitive options for reaching international markets.
The dredging initiative is also part of a wider modernization program under MPDC, whose concession to develop and operate the Port of Maputo has been extended to 2058, providing a longer investment horizon for the continued expansion of the facility.
DP World Deepens Investments in Mozambique’s Logistics Future
For DP World, the dredging initiative complements substantial investments in the development of the Port of Maputo’s container terminal, reinforcing the company’s growing role in Mozambique’s maritime and logistics sector.
The container terminal expansion is targeting an annual handling capacity of approximately 650,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), a development expected to improve cargo-handling capabilities and support growing trade volumes.
Alongside these improvements, the Matola coal terminal is targeting a capacity of 12 million tonnes, further strengthening the port complex’s ability to serve the region’s mining and bulk commodity industries.
Together, these investments are expected to improve operational efficiency, attract additional shipping services and strengthen Maputo’s competitiveness against other regional maritime gateways.
Akoojee emphasized the commercial opportunities that improved infrastructure could generate, noting that the investment would enable the port to serve larger vessels, connect Mozambique and neighboring markets more efficiently to continental and global trade, and create new opportunities for businesses across the region.
“We congratulate the MPDC for delivering this achievement and we thank Minister João Jorge Matlombe for his support in advancing this important project,” Akoojee said.
DP World’s involvement reflects the growing importance of integrated logistics solutions in Africa, where investment in ports is increasingly linked to inland transport corridors, industrial development and cross-border trade.
The Dubai-headquartered company operates an extensive international network of ports, terminals and logistics services, with a growing African footprint supporting trade, investment and supply-chain connectivity.
Its continued investments in Mozambique reinforce Maputo’s importance within that network and the company’s confidence in the country’s long-term commercial potential.
Southern Africa Poised to Benefit from Improved Trade Connectivity
The Port of Maputo’s expansion carries important implications for businesses operating across Southern Africa, particularly exporters and importers seeking efficient and competitive routes to international markets.
South Africa’s industrial heartland, including Gauteng and Mpumalanga, is connected to Mozambique through established transport corridors, while Eswatini and other neighboring economies also stand to benefit from improved maritime access and cargo-handling capacity.
For mining companies, agricultural exporters, manufacturers and logistics operators, improvements in port efficiency could contribute to reduced transportation bottlenecks, more reliable supply chains and stronger access to international buyers.
The project is also expected to reinforce the Maputo Development Corridor, a major regional trade route linking South Africa’s economic centers with Mozambique’s coastline.
The corridor has long played an important role in facilitating the movement of goods between the two countries, and improvements at the port could increase its attractiveness to businesses seeking alternative export and import routes.
Beyond Mozambique and South Africa, the investment has wider relevance for regional economic integration under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which seeks to expand trade among African economies and create a more integrated continental market.
While trade agreements can open commercial opportunities, their success depends heavily on efficient infrastructure, reliable transport networks and competitive logistics services.
The Maputo investment addresses an important part of that challenge by strengthening the maritime infrastructure needed to move goods between African markets and international trading partners.
President Chapo’s Government Pushes Infrastructure Development
The presence of President Daniel Chapo at the launch underscored the importance Mozambique attaches to modernizing its transport infrastructure and positioning the country as a competitive destination for investment and international trade.
Mozambique possesses significant natural resources, agricultural potential and a strategic coastline along the Indian Ocean. Its ports provide access to international shipping routes while serving neighboring economies that depend on efficient transport connections for their commercial activities.
However, realizing the full economic potential of these advantages requires sustained investment in infrastructure, institutional efficiency and partnerships capable of mobilizing long-term capital.
The Maputo dredging project represents an important example of collaboration between government authorities and private-sector operators in developing infrastructure critical to national and regional economic growth.
For the Chapo administration, the project also provides an opportunity to strengthen investor confidence, support industrial development and expand Mozambique’s participation in regional and international supply chains.
The benefits could extend beyond maritime operations, creating opportunities for freight forwarders, transport companies, warehousing operators and businesses providing services to the logistics sector.
The combination of deeper maritime access, expanded terminal capacity and improved regional connectivity could also help Mozambique attract additional commercial activity and investment in industries dependent on reliable export infrastructure.
Maputo Positions Itself Among Africa’s Competitive Maritime Gateways
Competition among African ports continues to intensify as governments and private operators invest in deeper channels, modern terminals, digital cargo systems and improved inland transport connections.
For shipping companies and international traders, the ability of a port to accommodate larger vessels, handle cargo efficiently and connect with major economic centers remains a decisive consideration.

Hello and welcome to The Core Report special edition.
I am joined today by Rahul Mithal, Chairman and Managing Director of RITES.
Let's find out more about the company, what it does, and why some of the things RITES is focusing on right now, including detailed project reports, are so critical at this time.
Thank you so much for joining me.
I am going to come to DPRs, or Detailed Project Reports, in a while, because that is really the foundation of everything you do.
But before that, tell us about what RITES does and how it was set up, for those who don't know.
Good morning.
RITES is a 52-year-young company.
It has a unique position in the infrastructure consultancy market: we are the only company in India, whether in the PSU space or the private infrastructure consultancy space, that has all areas of infrastructure under one roof, whether it is railways, ports, airports, highways, buildings, etc.
We have 13 different verticals, and we do three kinds of work primarily.
One is the DPR, the techno-economic feasibility report.
The second is project supervision, when the project is actually happening.
The third is third-party technical audits.
This 3-by-13 matrix makes us well equipped.
We are executing about 700-plus orders today, in the country and beyond.
We can proudly say that we are a one-order-a-day company, with a fresh order inflow of one order a day.
About 70–75% of these are on a competitive basis, both domestic and global.
When RITES was set up, it was obviously a subset of the Indian Railways, and you are also a railway man, so to speak.
Tell us about the breakup of orders today, both existing and current, between railway or railway-linked orders and non-railway orders.
Yes.
When RITES was incorporated in 1974, it was, and still is, a company with majority holding by the Ministry of Railways, so traditionally rail infrastructure consultancy was our core sector.
But very soon, right in the first decade, the founders had the vision and foresight to make RITES a core consultancy company across all sectors.
We started working with the Delhi Metro, and we were the initial consultants for it.
The Mumbai-Pune Expressway was one of the first highways, and RITES was the consultant for that.
Within the first year itself, we started doing international projects.
As I said, the railway sector accounts for about 30–35–40% of my total top line and bottom line.
But sectors like buildings, ports, airports and highways are also very important verticals for us, and they contribute to both revenue and bottom line.
How have things been shaping up in the last couple of years, given the geopolitical shifts we are seeing, particularly when it comes to global orders? I know you have been talking about consistency in orders from the Middle East despite all the trouble there.
And how has it been evolving in India, which of course has been seeing huge capital expenditure as a country? About two to two and a half years back, we were at about 0.
6 orders a day.
Gradually, market competition became much higher, and the era of giving PSUs work on a nomination basis was receding.
Our business re-engineering and our experience of 50-plus years made us very well equipped, and that is why we stepped up from 0.
6 to about one order a day.
We are now steadily maintaining that strike rate.
In some geographies there are ups and downs once in a while, but we still continue to get orders, both domestically and internationally.
In fact, we have pushed our international business arm, which covers both design and export of rolling stock as well as project consultancy.
In the last year we have opened five regional offices across various geographies of the world: Latin America, West Asia, two regions in the African continent, and one in Southeast Asia, in Manila.
That is the kind of push we have given to our international business.
If I were to ask you about this financial year, starting April 2026 as a start point, or even calendar year 2026, what would be the three or four most interesting projects that RITES has secured, whether in India or globally?Let me tell you about two or three key projects across my verticals.
In the rail infrastructure vertical, we are doing the feasibility study for a new high-speed corridor, the Chennai–Bangalore–Hyderabad high-speed corridor.
That is very exciting.
We had been associated with the earlier high-speed corridor, Mumbai–Ahmedabad.
We are also doing a lot of work in the metro sector.
While we were doing the Ahmedabad Metro and the Bangalore Metro, we most recently got the order for the Patna Metro.
We are also doing feasibility studies for metros across various geographies, for new metro corridors that are getting announced.
There is also the push for educational institutions like the IITs and IIMs, and we are proudly associated with premier institutions.
We are doing the expansion of IIT Delhi, IIM Bangalore, IIM Raipur and IIT Bhilai.
That is the kind of work we are doing in the building sector.
In.

In Tribute to the Late Rt. Hon. Raila Amolo Odinga: Celebrating Democratic Peace, Leadership and Africa’s Development
The 11th Annual London Political Summit and Awards (LPSA) 2026 concluded on Wednesday, 14 October 2026, following three days of high-level engagements involving political leaders, diplomats, government representatives, business stakeholders and civil society actors. Held in tribute to the late Rt. Hon. Raila Amolo Odinga, affectionately known as Baba, the Summit culminated in an International Awards Gala Dinner Reception celebrating outstanding leadership, democratic governance, peacebuilding and sustainable development.
The 2026 edition carried particular significance as it marked the first anniversary of the passing of Raila Odinga, the Summit’s late Global Grand Patron, whose legacy of Pan-Africanism, democratic reform, political reconciliation and regional cooperation continues to inspire leaders across Africa and beyond.
Her Excellency Amb. Irene the Deputy High Commissioner of Kenya to the United Kingdom receiving the Awards for Late Odinga and President Ruto, supported by Amb. Ojiambo.
The programme opened with a Business Dialogue at the Institute of Directors, London, on 12 October, followed by a special parliamentary session at the House of Commons, Westminster, on 13 October, hosted by the Rt. Hon. Oliver Ryan MP, Member of Parliament for Burnley. The Summit concluded with the International Awards Gala Dinner Reception at the Copthorne Tara Hotel, London Kensington, on 14 October.
Across the three days, discussions centred on Africa’s democratic and economic future, the relationship between peace and trade, accountable leadership, investment and stronger partnerships among governments, diplomatic missions, the private sector and development institutions.
A Solemn Tribute to Raila Odinga’s Democratic Legacy
A major highlight was the tribute to Raila Odinga delivered by Ambassador Dr. Josephine Ojiambo, former Kenya representative to the United Nations and former Commonwealth Deputy Secretary-General for Political Affairs, following a period of silence in his memory.
The Deputy Governor of Sokoto State HE. Engr. Gobir, receiving the Governor’s Award
The tribute, titled “Raila Amolo Odinga: A Life Given to Parliamentary Democracy,” reflected on his decades of public service, his struggle for multiparty democracy in Kenya, his years of detention without trial, and his commitment to constitutional reform and peaceful political change.
It recalled his service as Prime Minister of Kenya from 2008 to 2013, following the disputed 2007 elections, and his role in the power-sharing settlement that helped restore stability and paved the way for the landmark 2010 Constitution.
The tribute also highlighted his 2018 reconciliation with former President Uhuru Kenyatta, demonstrating his belief that political opponents could pursue dialogue rather than remain trapped in confrontation. Beyond Kenya, his work as the African Union’s High Representative for Infrastructure Development reflected his commitment to regional integration and stronger economic connections across the continent.
The tribute concluded that Raila Odinga’s enduring contribution was not simply his pursuit of political office, but his determination to strengthen the democratic institutions through which leaders are elected, held accountable and succeeded.
Hon. Dr. Margaret Adamu, receiving the Benue State Governor’s Award, with the state delegation
Parliamentary Session Brings Together Political and Diplomatic Leaders
The parliamentary session at the House of Commons provided a significant forum for reflecting on democratic governance, political reconciliation and the late statesman’s contribution to African democracy.
The session featured remarks from the Rt. Hon. Oliver Ryan MP and the Rt. Hon. Afzal Khan MP, alongside diplomatic representatives, government officials, traditional rulers, academics and business leaders.
Distinguished participants included the High Commissioner of The Gambia to the United Kingdom; representatives of the Kenya High Commission, including Deputy High Commissioner Ambassador Irene Maswan and Head of Chancery Mr. Alifo; representatives of the governments of Benue and Sokoto States in Nigeria; HRH Oba Ambassador Dr. Olusegun Aderemi JP; HRM Obongwanwan Marie Erete; Professor Kishan Devani BEM; and Ambassador Dr. Josephine Ojiambo.
Following the welcome remarks by the Rt. Hon. Oliver Ryan MP, the Rt. Hon. Afzal Khan MP delivered the opening address. Further contributions came from representatives of The Gambia and Ghana High Commissions, the Benue State Government, represented by Hon. International Awards Gala Celebrates Distinguished Leadership

articles.full_text:
Nigeria Targets New Maritime Hubs as Port Development Expands Beyond Lagos
Nigeria is pursuing a more geographically balanced port network, with plans to modernise existing maritime facilities and develop new deep seaports to strengthen trade, reduce logistics costs and stimulate economic activity beyond Lagos.
/ You Might Also Like /
The Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, reaffirmed the government's commitment to expanding maritime infrastructure outside the country's dominant commercial gateway during the 2026 World Maritime Day celebration in Lagos.
The programme includes modernisation plans for Onne, Warri and Calabar ports, complementing ongoing efforts at Apapa and Tin Can Island. The government has also identified proposed deep seaport projects at Agge, Bakassi, Bonny, Gateway, Ibom and Ondo.
The broader strategy aims to connect seaports with inland dry ports and production centres through an integrated network of roads, railways and inland waterways.
For Nigeria's property sector, the potential significance extends beyond maritime operations. If the infrastructure improvements translate into higher trade volumes, new businesses and employment, they could support demand for warehouses, industrial facilities, commercial premises and housing in regional economic centres.
Port Modernisation Targets Greater Regional Connectivity
Nigeria's port system remains heavily concentrated around Lagos, where Apapa, Tin Can Island and Lekki handle substantial volumes of the country's maritime trade.
Expanding capacity elsewhere could give importers and exporters more options for moving goods, while strengthening connections between coastal facilities and inland production and consumption centres.
The proposed modernisation of Onne, Warri and Calabar is part of this effort. The government also intends to advance new deep seaport projects, although the proposed developments will require further progress in financing, construction and supporting infrastructure before their full economic impact can be realised.
Oyetola said the strategy would connect maritime gateways to inland dry ports and production centres, bringing cargo closer to businesses and consumers while easing pressure on established transport corridors.
The effectiveness of this approach will depend on the quality of road and rail links, port operations, cargo-handling capacity and the efficiency of customs and other logistics processes.
Regional Ports Could Attract Industrial and Logistics Investment
More efficient ports can strengthen the commercial case for locating warehouses, distribution centres, processing facilities and industrial estates close to transport corridors.
Businesses that import equipment and raw materials or export finished goods often consider transport costs and reliability when choosing where to establish operations. Improved port access could make some regional locations more attractive if they offer dependable connections to suppliers, markets and labour.
Onne, Warri and Calabar could benefit from stronger demand for logistics and industrial facilities if port modernisation leads to sustained growth in cargo activity and related businesses.
New deep seaports could create similar opportunities in their host areas. However, infrastructure announcements alone do not guarantee new investment. Developers and businesses will also assess the availability of electricity, water, roads, serviced land, security and a suitable workforce.
For property investors, the distinction between planned infrastructure and operational capacity will be important when assessing the long-term potential of emerging logistics locations.
Housing Demand Could Follow Port-Linked Employment
Port development can influence residential property markets by attracting workers, contractors, logistics operators and businesses that require accommodation close to employment centres.
If improved maritime infrastructure generates sustained economic activity, host cities could experience increased demand for rental housing, serviced apartments and residential estates. Commercial expansion could also support demand for offices, retail premises and other services serving workers and businesses.
The potential effects may extend to surrounding communities connected to ports by major roads and transport networks. Locations that offer reliable access to employment centres could become more attractive to households and property developers.
However, additional economic activity can also place pressure on existing housing supply, land availability and public services. Without coordinated urban planning, new investment may contribute to higher land prices and rents without ensuring that lower-income workers can access adequate housing.
The housing impact of port expansion will therefore depend partly on whether local authorities and developers plan for worker accommodation, affordable housing, transport and essential services alongside industrial growth.
Inland Dry Ports Extend the Potential Impact Beyond Coastal Cities
The government's strategy also recognises the role of inland ports and waterways in connecting businesses outside coastal areas to domestic and international markets.
Facilities such as the inland ports at Onitsha and Baro could support the movement of goods between production centres, distribution networks and seaports. Their effectiveness will depend on operational capacity and dependable links to road, rail and water transport.
A more integrated logistics network could expand the locations suitable for warehousing, agro-processing, distribution and other industrial activities. It could also improve the commercial viability of property developments serving businesses along major freight routes.
For the property sector, these connections matter because industrial and logistics investment often depends on the entire transport network rather than the performance of an individual port.
Regulatory Reform Remains Part of the Port Development Agenda
Alongside infrastructure investment, Oyetola highlighted the Nigerian Ports Economic Regulatory Agency Act, 2026, as part of efforts to strengthen economic regulation, encourage fair competition and improve service delivery across the port system.
Effective regulation can influence operating costs, investor confidence and the consistency of services available to port users. These factors can affect whether businesses commit capital to new logistics and industrial locations.
Nevertheless, regulatory reform must translate into predictable processes, efficient operations and commercially viable services to support long-term investment.
For developers, the ability to assess infrastructure delivery, land access, transport connections and regulatory conditions will remain central to decisions about industrial and commercial property.
Infrastructure Delivery Will Determine Regional Property Opportunities
Nigeria's plan to expand port development beyond Lagos presents a potential opportunity to strengthen regional trade and encourage investment in logistics and industrial infrastructure.
Onne, Warri and Calabar are among the existing ports targeted for modernisation, while proposed deep seaports and inland transport connections form part of the wider strategy.
For real estate, the opportunity lies in the economic activity that functional infrastructure can generate: demand for warehouses, industrial sites, commercial premises and housing near expanding employment centres.
The scale of that opportunity will depend on project execution, reliable transport connections, private-sector participation and the availability of supporting urban infrastructure.
Until the projects deliver measurable improvements in cargo handling and business activity, anticipated property-market gains should be treated as potential rather than guaranteed outcomes.

articles.summary: Tony Elumelu Backs $15 Billion Investment Pipeline to Bridge West Africa's Infrastructure Deficit  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Nigerian billionaire and Heirs Holdings Chairman Tony Elumelu has formally backed a proposed $15 billion investment pipeline designed to systematically address the severe infrastructure deficit hindering economic growth across West Africa. The ambitious initiative aims to channel institutional and development capital into critical regional projects, moving beyond rhetoric to tangible financial execution.
Structuring the Investment Pipeline
Serving as the co-chair of the upcoming West Africa Integration and Investment Summit (WAIIS), Elumelu outlined the mechanics of the financing drive in communications with Bloomberg on October 15, 2026. The core strategy revolves around identifying commercially viable, large-scale infrastructure projects across multiple West African nations and presenting them to a consortium of heavyweight regional financiers.
The targeted financial partners include the United Bank for Africa (UBA), the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), the Africa Finance Corporation (AFC), and the pan-African infrastructure investment platform Africa50. By coordinating these institutions ahead of the inaugural summit scheduled for Sierra Leone in November, the initiative seeks to establish a unified front for project appraisal and capital deployment, significantly accelerating the financial close of critical public works.
Addressing West Africa's Infrastructure Deficit
The West African sub-region has long struggled with a profound infrastructure gap that severely limits industrialisation and intra-regional trade. Insufficient power generation, degraded transportation networks, and underdeveloped digital infrastructure consistently undermine the competitiveness of local enterprises. This deficit not only inflates the cost of doing business but also acts as a primary barrier to the successful implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Elumelu's intervention reflects a growing recognition that fragmented, country-by-country approaches to infrastructure development are insufficient. A regional pipeline approach allows for the pooling of resources and the development of cross-border infrastructure, such as transnational rail links, regional power pools, and interconnected digital backbones. These multi-country projects offer the scale necessary to attract significant institutional investment, which often bypasses smaller, isolated national projects.
The Role of Regional Financial Institutions
The success of the $15 billion pipeline depends heavily on the technical and financial capacity of the named partner institutions. Afreximbank and the AFC have established robust track records in structuring complex, multi-jurisdictional sovereign and corporate debt facilities. Their involvement provides the necessary de-risking mechanisms—such as political risk insurance and first-loss guarantees—that make these massive projects palatable to commercial banks and private equity funds.
United Bank for Africa (UBA), where Elumelu serves as Group Chairman, brings extensive regional market penetration, operating in twenty African countries. Its deep understanding of local regulatory environments and currency dynamics positions the bank to syndicate local currency financing, thereby reducing the severe foreign exchange risks that frequently destabilise long-term infrastructure investments in the region.
Accountability and Implementation Challenges
While the commitment to a $15 billion pipeline marks a significant milestone, the transition from capital commitments to completed infrastructure is fraught with operational challenges. Historical efforts to fund regional infrastructure have frequently stalled due to bureaucratic delays, inconsistent political will across bordering nations, and a lack of properly structured, bankable project pipelines.
This initiative also serves as a practical application of Africapitalism, an economic philosophy long championed by Elumelu. The doctrine argues that the African private sector possesses the unique capacity to generate both economic returns and broad social wealth through long-term investments in strategic sectors. By leading the charge to finance the region's physical foundation, the participating institutions are actively demonstrating how private capital can fulfill essential public needs while remaining commercially viable.
To overcome systemic hurdles, the WAIIS framework must enforce strict project preparation standards. Capital providers require comprehensive feasibility studies, transparent procurement processes, and guaranteed revenue models—such as tolling systems for roads or power purchase agreements for energy projects—before disbursing funds. Ensuring that sovereign governments respect these commercial agreements across decades-long investment horizons remains the ultimate test of the pipeline's viability.
| Key Institutional Partners in the West African Investment Pipeline |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Institution | Primary Financial Role | Strategic Contribution | 
|---|---|---|
| United Bank for Africa (UBA) | Commercial syndication and local currency structuring | Extensive regional footprint and deep local market liquidity | 
| Afreximbank | Trade finance and sovereign risk mitigation | Facilitation of cross-border trade infrastructure | 
| Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) | Project development and heavy infrastructure equity | Technical expertise in bridging early-stage project risks | 
| Africa50 | Project preparation and institutional capital mobilisation | Accelerating the financial close of mid-to-late stage projects | 
As the November summit in Sierra Leone approaches, the focus of the regional business community will be on the specific projects selected for this initial pipeline. If successfully executed, Elumelu's coordinated approach could establish a replicable blueprint for private sector-led infrastructure development, shifting the burden of regional integration away from constrained state budgets and towards disciplined, return-oriented capital.

The trade relationship between Ghana and the United Kingdom has crossed the GBP1.6 billion mark, with senior officials from both countries calling for deeper investment ties across agriculture, technology, manufacturing and the digital economy.
Alastair Long, His Majesty's Trade Commissioner for Africa, announced this during an interview at the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce's (UKGCC) Trade and Investment Summit 2026, held under the theme "A Decade of Trust, A Future Always On: Scaling the UK-Ghana Growth Partnership."
Long described the current bilateral relationship as a solid base for broader economic cooperation, stressing that the true measure of success lies not just in trade volumes but in the jobs and livelihoods that commercial activity generates on both sides.
He pointed to Ghanaian agricultural exports, including mangoes and bananas, as a growing presence on British shelves, and said both economies stand to gain from scaling up export flows while encouraging more UK businesses to plant roots in Ghana.
Delivering a keynote address on behalf of Vice President Prof. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, Deputy Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry Hon. Sampson Ahi told attendees that Ghana recorded GDP growth of 6 per cent in 2025, followed by a 6.4 per cent expansion in the first quarter of 2026.
"These numbers tell every investor in this room that Ghana is predictable, Ghana is stable, and Ghana is ready," he said.
Hon. Ahi shared that UK foreign direct investment in Ghana has reached GBP1.8 billion, backing more than 670 projects and creating upwards of 44,000 jobs.
He also drew attention to the newly signed UK-Ghana Growth Partnership for 2026 to 2028, describing it as a practical framework for accelerating industrial development and unlocking private-sector opportunities.
He urged investors to tap into Ghana's strategic location, its expanding workforce, and the preferential market access the country enjoys through the African Continental Free Trade Area.
"Bring your technology. Bring your patient capital. Bring your demand for quality and sustainability. In return, we offer a stable policy environment, a government that listens, and a people whose ingenuity has never been in short supply," he urged.
Ghana's High Commissioner urges quality over volume
Ghana's High Commissioner to the UK and the Republic of Ireland, Sabah Zita Benson, echoed calls for a partnership anchored in value addition, technology transfer and skills development rather than raw trade numbers.
She spotlighted Ghana's role as host of the AfCFTA Secretariat as a compelling incentive for UK investors seeking a gateway into the broader African market.
Benson also encouraged the Ghanaian diaspora in the UK to channel their expertise and networks into supporting development back home.
UKGCC Executive Director Adjoba Kyiamah, marking the chamber's tenth anniversary, said indigenous Ghanaian businesses should use the UK as a launchpad to access capital, expertise and global markets.
The three-day summit is backed by institutions including GCB Bank, PwC Ghana, Fidelity Bank Ghana, Ecobank Ghana, Guinness Ghana Breweries and Kasapreko, among others.
UK names new airport entry system
Earlier, YEN.com.gh reported that the UK had announced a new border entry system that would allow travellers to walk through airport eGates without touching a passport reader.
The phased rollout began on 6 October 2026 at East Midlands Airport and would initially cover British citizens. However, authorities expected the upgrade to reach all eligible airports by early 2027.

NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct. 15, 2026: Kenya will host an international energy conference in November aimed at addressing a central challenge for Africa’s clean energy ambitions: securing the financing and partnerships needed to turn renewable resources into operating projects and industrial growth.
The third KenGen Sustainable Energy Conference, scheduled for November 24 – 27 in Olkaria, Naivasha, is expected to attract more than 1,500 participants from over 80 countries. Organizers are targeting more than 200 investors, 40 financing institutions, 100 utilities and power producers, and 100 exhibitors.
Convened by the Kenya Electricity Generating Company, (KenGen), the gathering will bring project developers together with institutions that finance, regulate and buy electricity. Its theme, “Powering Africa’s Green Industrial Revolution,” places the commercial uses of clean energy at the center of the discussion.
For businesses considering where to build or expand, electricity supply is a practical investment decision. Reliability and cost affect production, competitiveness and the ability to plan. The conference will examine how renewable energy development can support those needs while helping companies reduce emissions.
“SEC 2026 is designed to move the green energy investment conversation from opportunity to execution,” said Eng. Kibet Ronoh, KenGen’s Ag. Managing Director and CEO, at the conference’s media launch in Nairobi. “We have invited investors, financiers, utilities, project developers and corporates to join us on this journey, and we are confident the conference will unlock meaningful opportunities that accelerate Africa’s clean energy agenda.”
The agenda will focus on investment mobilization, project development, strategic partnerships and carbon trading. Participants will include government officials, regulators, development finance institutions and companies seeking cleaner sources of power for their operations.
Bringing those groups together is intended to address the gap between identifying an energy opportunity and developing a project that can secure financing. Discussions will connect the requirements of investors and lenders with the needs of utilities, developers and industrial customers.
The location gives that discussion a working setting. Olkaria is the center of Kenya’s geothermal operations, allowing delegates to examine an established world-class renewable energy development alongside opportunities for further investment.
Participants will also learn about the KenGen Green Energy Park, which is intended to attract industries and enterprises seeking access to renewable electricity. The park connects the conference’s investment agenda with a broader economic question: how clean power can support production, enterprise and employment.
“Our guests will experience firsthand how strategic investments have driven growth in Olkaria,” Eng. Ronoh said. “They will also gain insight into how the KenGen Green Energy Park is creating new opportunities for industries and enterprises seeking reliable renewable energy solutions.”
KenGen said the conference would provide a platform for investment discussions and partnerships across Africa’s sustainable energy sector, with an emphasis on translating renewable energy potential into projects and productive economic activity.

October 16, 2026 by SIMEON EBULU, Group Business Editor and Collins Nweze | Assistant Business Editor
IMF urges Nigeria to raise non-oil revenue
•Fund backs CBN’s rate reset
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged the Federal Government to increase revenue from non-oil sources to create more resources for education, healthcare and infrastructure, while pursuing reforms to attract private investment and create jobs.
The Director of the IMF’s African Department, Zeine Zeidane, gave the advice during the presentation of the Fund’s Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa on the sidelines of the ongoing IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
The Fund also backed Central Bank of Nigeria’s gradual reduction of interest rates, saying the move is appropriate following significant progress in bringing inflation down, notwithstanding the fact that monetary policy remains tight.
Zeidane said Nigeria had made significant progress in reducing inflation after a period of high price increases, creating room for some adjustment in monetary policy.
He described the decision to reduce interest rates as appropriate but cautioned against interpreting it as a move towards an accommodative monetary policy.
According to him, the overall policy stance remained tight, suggesting that the authorities were adjusting monetary conditions gradually rather than abandoning efforts to control inflation.
The position provides an important signal for businesses and investors as they assess the likely direction of borrowing costs, credit conditions and economic activity in Nigeria.
This came as the CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, explained that he does not control Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) members decisions at policy meetings.
Speaking during a panel discussion at the ongoing World Bank-IMF meetings, he said MPC members speak freely and make contributions based on their convictions and knowledge of the issues at stake, adding, “I do not control how members speak”.
He described the MPC members as “independent-minded people,” who have their views and take that through life.
He said there’s never a case where he had meetings with internal staff and came to a conclusion on the MPC meetings before going there. “I don’t do that,” Cardoso said.
Speaking on the growth outlook, Deputy Director of the IMF’s African Department, Montfort Mlachila, said Nigeria’s economy was benefiting from improved oil prices, stronger foreign exchange earnings, higher external reserves and increased liquidity.
Mlachila said the Fund had raised its growth forecast for Nigeria to 4.2 per cent in 2026 from four per cent previously, while projecting growth of 4.3 per cent in 2027.
He attributed the improved outlook partly to the more favourable external environment, increased foreign exchange availability, falling inflation and the performance of the services sector.
The IMF’s assessment suggests that stronger oil earnings and improving macroeconomic conditions are supporting economic activity, although sustaining growth will require reforms that broaden the sources of government revenue and attract more investment.
Zeidane advised the Federal Government to mobilise more revenue from outside the oil sector to strengthen public finances and provide more resources for essential services.
He said higher domestic revenue would create fiscal space for investment in education, healthcare and infrastructure.
The advice comes against the background of Nigeria’s exposure to fluctuations in international oil prices and competing demands on government revenue.
Zeidane also called for continued structural reforms to improve governance, the business environment and Nigeria’s integration with international markets.
He said Nigeria had a large market, a dynamic population, young entrepreneurs and a technology-aware workforce that could make it attractive to private investors.
However, he said these advantages needed to be supported by reforms that would make it easier for businesses to invest, expand and create jobs.
The IMF’s recommendations place domestic revenue mobilisation and private-sector investment at the centre of Nigeria’s efforts to sustain economic growth.
Zeidane advised Nigeria and other African countries to protect vulnerable households from rising living costs through targeted assistance rather than broad fuel-price subsidies.
He said general energy subsidies were expensive and often benefited wealthier households more than poorer ones because higher-income earners generally consumed more fuel and energy.
In an illustrative scenario presented in the regional outlook, the IMF estimated that general fuel-price smoothing could cost about four per cent of gross domestic product (GDP). By contrast, targeted transfers providing the same benefit to the poorest 40 per cent of the population would cost no more than 0.5 per cent of GDP.
Zeidane said governments could consider alternatives such as school feeding and other targeted assistance where systems for identifying beneficiaries were weak.
He added that any temporary price relief should be transparently funded, limited in scope and time-bound.
The Fund said savings from subsidy reforms should be directed towards people who need assistance rather than being used to subsidise products in ways that weaken public finances.
Mlachila said Nigeria was benefiting from higher international oil prices, which had increased foreign exchange earnings and supported the accumulation of external reserves.
He said the improved foreign exchange position had also increased liquidity in the economy, helping to support growth.
The IMF’s assessment points to the importance of managing additional oil earnings carefully, particularly as the government faces competing demands for public services, infrastructure and debt payments.
Mlachila also identified the services sector as a major driver of Nigeria’s growth, alongside the benefits of the improved external environment.
Zeidane said Nigeria’s large market, young entrepreneurs and technology-aware population offered considerable opportunities for private investment.
However, he said the country needed to improve governance, strengthen the business environment and deepen its integration with international markets to unlock that potential.
He said reforms in these areas could accelerate economic growth and create jobs, particularly if they encouraged businesses to invest and expand.
Zeidane also advised African countries, including Nigeria, to develop stronger domestic financing sources and deepen their financial markets to improve access to affordable capital.
He said pension funds, insurance companies and other institutional investors could help broaden domestic debt markets and provide additional financing for productive activities.
The IMF raised its economic growth forecast for Sub-Saharan Africa to 4.5 per cent in both 2026 and 2027, an increase of 0.2 percentage point from its April projection.
Mlachila said the region’s resilience reflected earlier economic reforms and the ability of governments and businesses to adjust to global disruptions.
The reforms included subsidy and exchange rate changes in Nigeria and Ethiopia, as well as structural reforms in South Africa.
Businesses had also adapted by changing their supply sources and transport arrangements, while countries adjusted to disruptions in global energy supplies.
The Fund said these measures had helped the region withstand economic pressures better than might otherwise have been expected.
Despite the improved growth outlook, Zeidane warned that African economies remained exposed to fresh economic shocks.
He said a renewed disruption to energy supplies, a sharp rise in global financial market uncertainty or a severe El Niño weather event could increase pressure on economies.
The Fund warned that the effects of higher commodity prices differed across countries. Oil, copper and gold exporters were benefiting from stronger prices, while economies less dependent on natural resources were experiencing slower growth and widening external deficits.
For Nigeria, higher oil prices provide support, but the IMF’s broader warning suggests that stronger export earnings alone cannot remove the risks associated with global uncertainty.
The IMF projected that median inflation in the region would rise from 3.4 per cent in 2025 to 4.3 per cent in 2026 and five per cent in 2027.
Zeidane said fuel and transport costs had already increased, while higher fertiliser prices could raise food production costs and threaten food security.
The pressure could be particularly difficult for households already struggling with the cost of living.
Although the figures are regional projections rather than forecasts for Nigeria alone, the risks are relevant to the country because higher fuel, transport and agricultural input costs can feed into food prices and other household expenses.
Zeidane said earlier fiscal adjustments had helped African countries reduce their budget deficits and debt ratios, but their ability to respond to new shocks remained limited.
Interest payments absorb about 13 per cent of government revenue in a typical country in the region, leaving less money for social services and public investment.
He said borrowing costs remained high even though some countries had continued to access international capital markets.
The IMF also warned that increased government borrowing from domestic banks could reduce credit available to businesses and deepen the link between government finances and the banking sector.
For Nigeria, the broader concern is the need to balance debt servicing with spending on infrastructure, education, healthcare and other productive activities.
Mlachila said countries across the region had issued about $12 billion in international bonds during the first nine months of the year.
He explained that economic reforms had helped several countries reduce the additional interest investors demanded to lend to them.

articles.title: Inside the 18th BRICS Summit: Trade wars, de-dollarization and India’s strategic autonomy - ET Government
articles.summary: Inside the 18th BRICS Summit: Trade wars, de-dollarization and India’s strategic autonomy  ET Government
articles.full_text:
The Western bloc itself shows visible disunity amidst these tariff wars and military disputes. While the US once held undisputed global dominance, various emerging powers are challenging American supremacy, signaling a shift toward a multipolar world order. Nevertheless, the US continues to operate as a superpower, even as its military, economic, and diplomatic influence wanes in certain respects.
Numerous global blocs operate today, including the G7, G20, NATO, the European Union, ASEAN, the Quad, BRICS, and the GCC. The US, European Union, G7, and NATO are generally regarded as powerful Western blocs, though President Trump remains at odds with NATO. Meanwhile, observers view the growing influence of BRICS as the rise of forces opposed to the US.
Furthermore, the US shows reluctance to abide by the rules of the World Trade Organization (WTO)—an institution established largely through American initiative—and fails to provide necessary contributions, causing the dispute settlement mechanism to grind to a halt. Consequently, the WTO faces a slow demise due to US tariffs and impasses that run counter to its framework.
As major global powers engage in economic and military conflicts, the rise of China as an economic and military force is actively shifting the global balance of power. Against this backdrop, understanding the agenda and India's role in the ongoing 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi becomes essential.
BRICS initially formed as an informal group of four nations—Brazil, Russia, India, and China—known as BRIC, before renaming itself to BRICS following South Africa's inclusion. With the recent addition of six members—Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates—the grouping has evolved into an expanded BRICS.
Russia and China continue to advocate for de-dollarization at BRICS summits, and Brazil largely adopts an anti-US stance. In contrast, India's posture toward the US remains non-hostile. India consistently maintains that it does not oppose any nation's currency; rather, it opposes the weaponization of payment systems, global value chains, essential raw materials, or technology.
India advocates for conducting trade in local currencies wherever possible and desires an end to global conflicts so the world can advance through peace and coexistence—a position it repeatedly raises in bilateral talks and global forums. Furthermore, India actively strives to conduct trade in rupees with as many partner nations as possible, achieving notable success.
India's Priorities
As host of the Delhi Summit, India faces the central challenge of advancing issues concerning global peace, harmony, development, and survival. Attention centers on promoting green energy and infrastructure development through the New Development Bank, alongside expanding trade in local currencies. India aims to position itself as a leading voice for the Global South while maintaining its strategic autonomy.Digital Public Infrastructure. India is offering BRICS partners cooperation across digital payments, digital identity, digital commerce, digital health, digital skills, cybersecurity, and AI.energy security remains a vital focal point. India is actively collaborating with global partners across solar, nuclear, and wind sectors, utilizing the ongoing BRICS meetings to advance clean energy cooperation.Challenges for India
Discussions at the summit inevitably touch upon US tariff policies, trade restrictions, and military action against Iran. Russia and China prioritize de-dollarization, while newly admitted Iran participates in efforts aimed at countering Washington. India—which neither fully aligns with Russia and China nor supports Donald Trump's policy actions—faces the delicate task of securing a universally accepted joint declaration.
(The author is  National Co-convenor, Swadeshi Jagaran Manch and Former Professor, PGDAV College, University of Delhi; Views expressed are personal)

The proposed investment would be deployed as opportunities arise, with the company pursuing port concessions and logistics projects, including the proposed Vadhavan port on the western coast. Narayan said the amount was not tied to a fixed investment timetable and would depend on the outcome of bids.
"We are prepared to invest between $3 billion and $5 billion (in India)," he told a select group of journalists.
DP World, which has built an integrated Indian network spanning ports, rail and inland logistics, is seeking to expand its footprint as the world's most populous country looks to strengthen domestic connectivity and become a larger manufacturing and export hub.
The company announced an additional $5 billion India investment commitment in October 2025, over and above $3 billion invested in the country over three decades.
India's infrastructure push has delivered substantial improvements, Narayan said, but port and rail development and the processes governing project execution need to move faster.
"One always hopes things could happen faster," he said, pointing to the long wait for the Vadhavan project and arguing that infrastructure development should keep pace with progress in roads, airports and power.
DP World is prepared to bid for new opportunities, expand its rail network and increase port capacity, Narayan said. The company currently operates six port concessions in India and plans to increase its railheads from eight to 12, according to him.
India's growing economic scale makes it attractive despite historically weaker returns on invested capital, Narayan said. Currency depreciation, driven in part by the country's energy import bill, has weighed on returns, while infrastructure upgrades, digitisation and the shift towards renewable energy could improve the outlook.
The proposed investment would also help strengthen DP World's wider supply-chain network, rather than simply expand its Indian business, he said.
The investment push comes as disruptions around key West Asian maritime chokepoints force shipping companies to reroute cargo, add capacity and absorb higher operating costs.
Narayan said DP World's flagship Jebel Ali port in Dubai, which normally handles about 15 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) annually, was facing a severe reduction in activity because of restricted access. He said the disruption was affecting cargo flows well beyond the Gulf, creating congestion at ports and logistics facilities across parts of Asia and Africa.
The impact extends beyond the port itself, he said, because Jebel Ali serves as a major transshipment hub linking Asian manufacturing centres with markets in the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
DP World had expected Jebel Ali's port operations to generate about $1.2 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), but Narayan said the disruption would materially reduce the group's earnings outlook. He estimated that global EBITDA could fall to about $5.8 billion from a level of roughly $6.2 billion to $6.4 billion, with growth elsewhere cushioning part of the lost contribution.
The company is exploring alternative routes through other Gulf ports and overland connections, including routes through Saudi Arabia, Narayan said. But building replacement capacity takes time, and he estimated that new port capacity could take two to three years to develop.
"Port capacity is not created overnight," he said, warning that the full consequences of the disruption may take time to emerge.
The crisis also underscores the growing cost of building redundancy into supply chains. Companies that once prioritised lean inventories, low costs and just-in-time deliveries are increasingly seeking alternative suppliers, routes and production centres to reduce their exposure to geopolitical shocks.
Narayan said global trade now required substantially more shipping capacity to move less cargo than before, as longer routes and operational inefficiencies absorbed available capacity. Higher interest rates, fuel expenses and other operating costs were adding to the burden.
"Who do you think pays for all this disruption? You - as a consumer," he said, arguing that the additional costs would ultimately be passed through to buyers of goods.
He expects shorter supply chains and a greater emphasis on regional production to reshape trade flows over time, potentially increasing the importance of north-south trade between Asia, Africa and other emerging markets.
For India, the opportunity lies in expanding manufacturing and exports while building the port, rail and inland logistics infrastructure needed to connect producers with global markets.
Narayan said India's exports and imports currently account for a relatively small share of its overall economy, leaving considerable room for growth. A substantial increase in trade would require a corresponding expansion in logistics capacity, he said.
However, he cautioned that resilience would come at a cost. Maintaining alternative routes, suppliers and inventory buffers would make supply chains more expensive and capital-intensive than the lean systems businesses had previously pursued.
"The world has to come to peace," Narayan said, arguing that physical infrastructure alone cannot eliminate the risks posed by conflict.

articles.summary: Egypt becomes last original signatory to ratify D-8 trade pact  Yeni Şafak English
articles.full_text:
Egypt has formally ratified the D-8 Preferential Trade Agreement, making all eight original signatories, including Türkiye, full participants in the pact signed in Bali in 2006. The D-8 Secretariat says the step gives fresh momentum to the bloc’s US$500 billion intra-D-8 trade target for 2030, while member states are now exploring a wider Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
Egypt has ratified the D-8 Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA), completing the ratification process for all eight original signatory states of the Developing-8 Organization for Economic Cooperation. Cairo formally handed its Instrument of Ratification to the D-8 Secretariat in Istanbul in October 2026, joining Bangladesh, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Türkiye, which have all completed their own procedures.
From the Bali signing to full ratification
The agreement was signed on 13 May 2006 at the Fifth D-8 Summit in Bali, Indonesia, entered into force on 25 August 2011, and began to be implemented on 1 July 2016. Egypt’s ratification date is 16 June 2026, with the instrument deposited with the Secretariat in October. The D-8 describes the PTA as a flagship instrument of its economic cooperation, providing for preferential tariff reductions, improved market access and easier trade facilitation.
Secretary-General welcomes the step
D-8 Secretary-General Ambassador Sohail Mahmood welcomed the development and thanked the Egyptian government and all original signatories for their steady commitment to the organization’s shared goals of closer economic cooperation and trade expansion. The Secretariat says effective implementation of the PTA can boost intra-D-8 trade, strengthen regional value chains and open new opportunities for businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises.
Eyes on the $500 billion trade target
The Secretariat says the milestone gives fresh impetus to the bloc’s target of US$500 billion in intra-D-8 trade by 2030 under the D-8 Decennial Roadmap 2020-2030. Building on the Cairo Declaration on D-8 Trade Cooperation, adopted in December 2025, member states are exploring a broader trade framework, including the possibility of a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
Next steps for the Secretariat
The D-8 Secretariat, based in Istanbul, says it will keep working with member states on effective PTA implementation, wider preferential trade coverage, stronger customs cooperation and greater private-sector participation. The organization describes the completed ratification by all original signatories as “a new chapter in translating the D-8’s collective economic potential into tangible benefits for its Member States and their people.”
