articles.title: UI VC, Dons, IMF official seek solutions to Nigeria’s economic challenges - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: UI VC, Dons, IMF official seek solutions to Nigeria’s economic challenges  The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.full_text:
Vice-Chancellor, University of Ibadan (UI), Prof. Kayode Adebowale; scholars from the institution and an official of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Dr. Afolabi Olowookere, have called for research-driven solutions to Nigeria’s economic challenges, including inflation, poverty, unemployment, inadequate electricity supply and low productivity.
The UI dons include the former president of the Nigerian Economic Society [NES], Prof. Adeola Adenikinju; the Dean of the Faculty of Economics and Management Sciences, Prof. Akanni Lawanson, and others.
Adebowale, Adenikinju and Lawanson made the call at the maiden International Conference on Economics, Finance and Business organised by the university’s Faculty of Economics and Management Sciences at the Central Bank of Nigeria Building, UI.
The conference, themed: “Navigating Global Economics and Financial Disruptions,” brought together scholars, policymakers and practitioners to examine economic uncertainty, financial instability, international trade, technological innovation and sustainable development.
Also present at the conference were Prof. Juwon Arotiba; Prof. Abiodun Folawewo, Dr. Samuel Orekoya, Dr. Oluseyi Ajayi, Dr. Philips Ogunode, Dr. Adeola Ayodele, Dr. Roseline Ozegbe, Mrs. Ibukun Joledo and others.
Speaking at the event, the VC, Adebowale, urged economists and business scholars to develop evidence-based recommendations that could help policymakers address the country’s economic difficulties and promote inclusive growth.
He said universities had a responsibility not only to generate knowledge but also to help society understand complex economic developments, formulate sound policies and develop practical responses to contemporary challenges.
According to him, research conducted in Nigerian universities should go beyond theoretical discussions to provide evidence that could help policymakers understand the causes of economic problems, assess alternative interventions and identify sustainable pathways to economic growth.
He identified productivity, inflation, employment, exchange-rate stability, food security, industrial development and economic diversification as areas requiring rigorous research.
The Vice-Chancellor also highlighted the importance of a resilient financial system in supporting investment, improving access to credit, encouraging entrepreneurship and facilitating the growth of productive enterprises.
He urged stronger collaboration among universities, government agencies, financial institutions, private-sector organisations and international partners, adding that research findings should be communicated through policy briefs, public lectures and stakeholder engagements.
In his keynote address, the former president of the Nigerian Economic Society, Adenikinju, called for a balanced assessment of President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, warning that improvements in some macroeconomic indicators had yet to translate into meaningful relief for many households.
Adenikinju said Nigeria was experiencing a contrast between improving economic indicators and persistent hardship among citizens.
He cited rising foreign reserves alongside increasing poverty as evidence of the need to assess economic performance beyond headline figures.
The don identified dependence on crude oil, inadequate electricity supply, weak agricultural productivity and widespread informal employment as major constraints to inclusive economic growth.
Drawing lessons from South Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia, Botswana and Mauritius, he said Nigeria could improve its economic prospects by investing in agriculture, infrastructure, skills development and export-oriented production.
He proposed a Nigeria Competitiveness Compact built around macroeconomic stability, improved power supply and logistics, value addition to agricultural and mineral resources, skills development, artificial intelligence, production financing and export expansion under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Adenikinju urged economists and academics to provide independent, evidence-based assessments of government policies, stressing that the success of reforms should ultimately be measured by their impact on productivity, employment and living standards.
Also speaking, the IMF Executive Director (Alternate) for West Africa, Dr. Olowookere, identified reliable electricity, effective implementation of AfCFTA and access to sustainable financing as critical to strengthening Africa’s competitiveness.
Olowookere, who addressed the conference virtually, said global disruptions were increasingly affecting African economies through rising food and energy prices, mounting debt-servicing costs and employment challenges.
He identified geopolitics, changing trade rules, artificial intelligence, the energy transition, high debt levels and climate change as six forces reshaping the global economy.
According to him, African countries must develop the capacity to turn these disruptions into opportunities through macroeconomic stability, credible institutions, reliable power and logistics, technological skills, regional economic integration and access to long-term financing.
He urged African governments to invest in locally developed artificial intelligence solutions to address challenges in agriculture, healthcare, education and tax administration rather than remain consumers of imported technologies.
The IMF official also stressed that dependable electricity and efficient logistics were essential to lowering production costs, improving productivity and enabling African businesses to compete effectively in regional and international markets.
On AfCFTA, he said effective implementation, interoperable payment systems and harmonised standards would help businesses operate across national borders and gain access to a wider continental market.
Olowookere also called for more sustainable financing arrangements to support productive investment and reduce African economies’ vulnerability to external shocks.
The Dean of the Faculty of Economics and Management Sciences, Prof. Akanni Lawanson, said the conference was designed to position the faculty at the centre of national economic debate and policy formulation.
Lawanson also called for a balanced assessment of the Federal Government’s reforms, noting that while some macroeconomic indicators had improved, households and businesses continued to face high living costs, borrowing expenses and other economic pressures.
He said reforms should be assessed according to their ability to deliver structural transformation and tangible improvements in citizens’ welfare.
The Secretary to the Oyo State Government, Prof. Musibau Babatunde, said infrastructure investment must be linked to productivity, while farmers required adequate security to protect themselves and their crops.

The National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) has officially joined the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), marking a significant milestone in the country’s efforts to modernize its financial sector and strengthen economic integration with African markets.
The development, announced by PAPSS on Thursday, is expected to facilitate cross-border transactions, reduce payment costs, and enhance trade and investment opportunities between Ethiopia and other African countries.
PAPSS enables businesses and financial institutions across participating African countries to conduct transactions directly in local currencies, reducing dependence on the US dollar and eliminating the need for intermediary correspondent banks traditionally used to process international payments.
National Bank of Ethiopia Governor Eyob Tekalign welcomed the development, emphasizing that Ethiopia’s participation in PAPSS represents an important step toward modernizing the country’s financial system and strengthening its economic ties with the rest of Africa.
Launched in January 2022 with an initial network of 10 commercial banks, PAPSS has expanded significantly and now operates in more than 15 African countries, including Nigeria, Kenya, Zambia, Malawi, and Tunisia. The platform currently connects more than 150 commercial banks across the continent, although South Africa has yet to join the network.
The payment system also plays a key role in supporting the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) by facilitating more efficient, affordable, and accessible cross-border payments.
Ethiopia’s integration into PAPSS represents another step in the country’s ongoing financial sector reforms and broader efforts to enhance regional trade, promote financial connectivity, and deepen economic cooperation across Africa.
The move is expected to create new opportunities for Ethiopian businesses and financial institutions to participate more actively in intra-African trade while supporting the country's growing integration into the continental financial system.

articles.summary: CLARENCE TSHITEREKE | Mining renewal as a national growth strategy  Business Day
articles.full_text:
At the Johannesburg Indaba on October 7 Minerals Council South Africa president Paul Dunne argued that mining’s renewal is integral to overcoming low growth, unemployment and declining investor confidence.
He placed mining within a national growth agenda based on its mineral endowment, export strength, investment potential and employment multipliers. Realising this potential depends on converting geological advantage into investable, internationally competitive projects.
The urgency follows from South Africa’s labour market crisis. Dunne noted that 8.5-million people are unemployed and about 300,000 net new work seekers enter the labour market annually, while the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts growth of just 1% this year, far below the 3% needed to absorb new entrants. Poverty reduction therefore requires sustained growth and expanding productive employment.
Mining generates value across the wider economy. In 2025 it was South Africa’s largest source of export earnings, contributing R814bn and vital foreign exchange. It also mobilises investment in engineering, equipment, transport, energy, maintenance, professional services and local procurement.
Dunne observed that each mining job generates about 10 upstream jobs. Each employee supports 5-10 dependants, while average monthly earnings of R37,000 place mining among the country’s better-paying sectors.
These relationships make mining particularly relevant to employment absorption. Mining jobs support households, local demand and supplier networks, while continued or expanded operations can sustain communities in regions with few alternatives.
Dunne therefore positioned mining growth as a national imperative, delivering direct employment, upstream linkages, export revenues, capital formation and productive capacity.
The address also identified grounds for optimism. Minerals Council members have announced mine life extensions, new mines and progress in feasibility studies. PwC’s SA Mine 2026 report records a significantly expanded reserve base in gold, platinum group metals and iron ore, supported by higher prices, technology and existing infrastructure as well as R70bn in committed investment ready for implementation.
Though most will maintain current output, this remains economically meaningful: it preserves skilled employment, exports, supplier contracts and industrial capacity in an industry where mines have finite lives and capital is mobile.
These developments show that South Africa’s mining potential is not exhausted. Its exceptional mineral endowment, expertise and industrial capability position it to supply minerals for industrial development, energy security, advanced manufacturing and technology. The question is whether its institutional and infrastructure environment can convert these resources into investable projects.
Dunne’s diagnosis was direct. Mining production remains below levels achieved more than two decades ago. Exploration expenditure has declined by 80% over that period, and South Africa attracts less than 1% of global exploration capital despite its exceptional geology. Because exploration underpins future production, this decline means fewer discoveries, mines, investments, jobs and export earnings.
These shortcomings cannot be attributed to poor geology, weak resources or absent investor interest. The constraints are systemic. Mining investment depends on reliable infrastructure, efficient permitting, predictable regulation, adequate water and electricity, effective administration and secure operations.
Logistics failures, utility shortages, crime, illegal mining and uncertainty in policy and mineral rights administration increase costs and risk, weakening project economics and South Africa’s appeal relative to competing jurisdictions.
The Minerals Council’s investment and growth strategy responds to this reality. Developed with more than 20 mining CEOs, council leadership, 30 member-company representatives and investors, it shows that mining’s constraints span institutions.
Reform cannot unlock investment while barriers persist in logistics, energy, water, administration and regulation. Effective action therefore requires co-ordination across government, regulators, state-owned entities and business.
Dunne emphasised mining’s inclusion in the third phase of the presidency’s government-business partnership, supported through Operation Vulindlela. Alongside agriculture and tourism, mining is recognised as capable of rapidly unlocking growth constraints.
The partnership seeks annual growth above 3% and 1-million additional jobs by 2030. Mining’s inclusion reflects its scale, investment potential and economic multipliers, while providing a practical implementation framework.
Operation Vulindlela can align government, regulators, state-owned entities and business around measurable objectives. Its first workstream targets administrative bottlenecks and aims to unlock more than R50bn in capital expenditure by February 2028.
The pipeline already includes new investments, expansions and mine-life extensions. The task is to remove obstacles preventing viable projects from being approved and implemented.
The second workstream addresses reforms needed to strengthen South Africa’s competitiveness as a mining destination. Mobile international capital weighs institutional performance, administrative efficiency, transparency and regulatory predictability alongside resource endowment.
Processing applications, administering mineral rights and maintaining reliable operating conditions determine whether long-term capital is committed. A successful Mineral Resources Development Amendment Bill is therefore part of a broader competitiveness agenda.
The third workstream supports the department of mineral and petroleum resources in implementing a transparent, efficient national mining cadastre by March 2027. Fundamental to modern mineral-rights administration, it would reduce uncertainty and assure investors of a fair and predictable framework.
For a country attracting less than 1% of global exploration capital, this system is central to rebuilding future investment. The prospective gains are substantial. Minerals Council analysis indicates that sustained annual mining growth of 3% could add about R65bn to real GDP and support 50,000-100,000 additional jobs by 2035.
This explains mining’s place in the national growth agenda: a larger, more productive sector would strengthen exports, deepen industrial linkages, generate better paying employment and improve labour market absorption.
If Operation Vulindlela delivers, the result would extend beyond improved mining sentiment to a more credible investment environment where projects move into construction and production. The targeted R50bn could support new and expanded operations, preserve mine life and, alongside a functional cadastre, strengthen exploration confidence.
Better regulatory administration, more reliable infrastructure and lower operating uncertainty could reduce the risk premium associated with South African mining. These improvements would reinforce one another, converting mineral potential into productive assets and productive assets into exports, incomes and jobs.
Dunne’s address made the case for conditional optimism. South Africa’s mineral wealth remains a major advantage, and recent investment signals show renewed growth is possible. The decisive issue is whether government and business can enable capital deployment, efficient permitting, transparent rights administration and competitive operations.
The government-business partnership and Operation Vulindlela offer the clearest immediate mechanism, capable of positioning mining as a durable engine of investment, employment and national prosperity.
- Dr Tshitereke, an honorary professor at Unisa’s Thabo Mbeki School of Public and International Affairs, is chief of staff at the mineral and petroleum resources ministry.

articles.title: Andrew Milne, the fintech founder who helped bring credit to small businesses, dies at 54 - TechCabal
articles.summary: Andrew Milne, the fintech founder who helped bring credit to small businesses, dies at 54  TechCabal
articles.full_text:
Andrew Milne, the Kuunda co-founder who helped build the technology connecting banks to small businesses and mobile money users across Africa, died on October 13, the company said. He was 54.
Only days earlier, he celebrated completing a secondary share sale for the business he helped start in 2018. It was a moment to look ahead for Kuunda, as its early investors were seeing a return and the company was preparing for another phase of growth.
Now, his colleagues must carry those plans forward without him.
“Andy was an energetic and resilient leader,” Kuunda said in a statement. “He was much loved and deeply respected by everyone who worked alongside him.”
The company did not disclose the cause of death.
Milne founded Kuunda in 2018 with Sam Brawerman and Morné van der Westhuizen. Their starting point was a persistent cash flow problem that mobile money agents, small businesses, and consumers face despite being connected to digital payment networks. The team began designing its first liquidity product in Tanzania.
Kuunda built technology that allowed banks and digital platforms to offer credit within services people already used. The company used transaction data to help assess borrowers and embed overdrafts and working capital into services they already used.
It was work that could reach millions of people without making the company behind it a household name.
“We’re a media-shy company,” Milne told Techpoint Africa in a 2025 interview. Among Kuunda’s earliest partners was M-PESA Tanzania, where it helped develop financing for mobile money agents before extending its work into other lending products.
Before Kuunda, Milne had worked in mobile health and financial services. He was managing director of Virgin Lifecare and later chief executive of Hello Doctor, which connected people to medical expertise through their phones. He subsequently served as chief operating officer at mobile money company Zoona.
Those businesses addressed different needs, but each involved finding ways to deliver services beyond the reach of conventional branches and consulting rooms.
At Kuunda, that approach grew into a business spanning African and Asian markets. In October 2025, the company announced a $7.5 million pre-Series A round, following its expansion from Tanzania and Pakistan into Uganda, Malawi, Kenya, and Mozambique.
Its latest transaction, a $5 million secondary share sale announced on October 13, allowed early investors to sell shares to a group led by E4E Africa. Existing backers Accion Ventures, Portugal Gateway Fund, and Seedstars Africa Ventures increased their holdings.
For his colleagues, that milestone is now bound up with their last memories of him at work.
“Kuunda’s next chapter will now be written without him, and we will carry it forward in a way that honours what he started,” the company said.
Milne is survived by his wife, Alison, and their children.

articles.title: Egypt, Thailand sign 3 cooperation deals at 1st joint committee meeting in 20 years - Foreign Affairs - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Egypt, Thailand sign 3 cooperation deals at 1st joint committee meeting in 20 years - Foreign Affairs - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Egypt and Thailand signed three cooperation instruments in Bangkok on Thursday, including a 2027–2029 joint action plan, as their joint ministerial committee met for the first time in 20 years.
The committee’s third session, following the previous meeting in Cairo in 2006, came during the first ministerial visit to Thailand by an Egyptian foreign minister in three decades.
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty co-chaired the session with Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, according to an Egyptian foreign ministry statement.
Alongside the joint action plan, the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding on cultural cooperation and another between the Egyptian Agency of Partnership for Development and the Thailand International Cooperation Agency.
They also agreed to finalize an agreement on reciprocal visa exemptions for holders of diplomatic, official, mission, and special passports.
Foreign Ministry Spokesman Nader Zaki said Abdelatty called for increasing and diversifying bilateral trade, improving access for Egyptian exports to Thailand, and encouraging companies to explore joint investment opportunities.
The minister highlighted investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, saying Egypt’s location and infrastructure could help Thai companies reach African, Arab, and European markets. He also urged the Egyptian-Thai Business Council to play a more active role in developing investment partnerships.
The economic discussions followed industrial cooperation talks earlier this week.
On political relations, FM Abdelatty welcomed the eighth round of bilateral consultations held in Cairo in June 2026 and expressed interest in convening the ninth round in Thailand. He called for regular high-level visits and consideration of additional consultation mechanisms.
Earlier this week, the minister also held talks with parliamentarians in Bangkok.
Abdelatty praised Princess Sirivannavari’s attendance at the Grand Egyptian Museum’s opening, describing it as a reflection of the cultural and people-to-people ties between the two countries.
He also welcomed his Thai counterpart’s initiative to relaunch the Thailand–Africa Initiative, saying cooperation with Egypt could support wider Thai engagement in Africa in line with the African Union’s Agenda 2063 and the priorities of countries of the Global South.
Regional discussions covered efforts to complete the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan. Abdelatty stressed the need to fulfil all first-phase commitments, including ensuring unhindered humanitarian aid deliveries and advancing early recovery.
Egypt has repeatedly pressed for unhindered access for aid. In a separate interview this week, Abdelatty held Israel responsible for delays in implementation.
The ministers also discussed regional escalation and its implications for energy security and supply chains. Abdelatty called for intensified efforts to contain tensions, prevent the conflict from spreading, and safeguard freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz.
The talks also addressed the Ethiopian dam, Egyptian water security, and developments in the Horn of Africa and Red Sea.
Egypt’s top diplomat reiterated that Nile water is an existential issue for Egypt and rejected unilateral measures in the Eastern Nile Basin that contravene international law.
Egypt and Thailand established diplomatic relations in 1954. Agreements covering trade, investment protection, culture, and education underpin their cooperation. Meanwhile, Al-Azhar, the world’s most prominent Sunni Islamic institution, has long provided scholarships and religious education to Thai Muslim students.
Thailand and Egypt established the bilateral cooperation commission through an exchange of letters in September 1989.
Bilateral trade reached $974.86 million in 2025, according to Thailand’s foreign ministry, which identified Egypt as Thailand’s largest trading partner in North Africa.
In February 2026, a Thai business delegation visited Cairo for a bilateral business forum and meetings focused particularly on food processing, investment opportunities, and supply chains.
Thai industrial investment includes Hi-Tech Apparel’s $20 million sportswear factory in Qantara West, within the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
At the groundbreaking ceremony in April 2025, the zone’s authority said the project would create about 2,000 direct jobs and produce six million garments annually at full capacity, primarily for European and American markets.

articles.title: Afreximbank Targets $3.2bn Investment Opportunities at C’River Conference - THISDAYLIVE
articles.summary: Afreximbank Targets $3.2bn Investment Opportunities at C’River Conference  THISDAYLIVE
articles.full_text:
Latest Headlines
Afreximbank Targets $3.2bn Investment Opportunities at C’River Conference
Funmi Ogundare
Afreximbank, in partnership with the Cross River State Government, the Nigeria Governors’ Forum and the Forum of State Investment Promotion Agencies in Nigeria, will convene the sixth African Sub-Sovereign Governments Network Investment Conference (AfSNET) in Calabar from November 12 to 14, 2026, as the state intensifies efforts to attract investment and expand agricultural production.
The conference, scheduled to hold at the Calabar International
Centre, will focus on mobilising investment, developing bankable projects and strengthening intra-African trade.
It comes as Cross River secured a commitment of more than $20 million from ValueFronteira Limited to develop a 4,000-hectare oil palm plantation in Yala Local Government Area over five years.
A statement by Afreximbank said AfSNET had facilitated more than $3.2 billion in investment opportunities and transactions since its establishment in 2021. The network has convened more than 1,400 delegates across five editions, with 21 African countries represented.
The sixth edition, themed “The Role of Sub-Sovereigns in Catalysing Development Through Trade and Investment,” is expected to bring together African sub-national governments, investors, financial institutions and development partners to advance investment-ready projects, partnerships and intra-African trade opportunities.
The three-day programme will feature investment promotion training, project preparation workshops, investment showcases, discussions on Special Economic Zones, business-to-government deal rooms and investment pitch sessions designed to connect sub-national governments directly with financiers and investors.
Speaking on the conference, Cross River State Governor, Senator Bassey Otu, said hosting the event would provide the state with an opportunity to engage African and international investors, showcase its investment opportunities and build partnerships to support sustainable economic development.
“Hosting the sixth AfSNET Investment Conference provides Cross River State with an important opportunity to engage African and international investors, demonstrate the breadth of investment opportunities within the state and build partnerships that can support sustainable economic development,” he said. Otu said the state looked forward to welcoming governments, businesses, financiers and development partners to Calabar.
Also speaking, Afreximbank’s Executive Vice-President, Intra-African Trade and Export Development, Mrs Kanayo Awani, said sub-sovereign governments were central to Africa’s economic transformation because much of the continent’s production, infrastructure development and investment took place at that level.
She said AfSNET provided a platform for states, provinces and counties to strengthen project preparation, connect viable opportunities with capital and build the productive capacity needed to expand intra-African trade.
“The sixth AfSNET Investment Conference will therefore place particular emphasis on bankable projects, investment mobilisation and partnerships that can support industrialisation, value addition and stronger regional value chains,” Awani added.
Among the investment opportunities associated with the network is the $40 million Med Aditus Pharmaceuticals project in Kisumu, Kenya. The project, which is under preparation, envisages a manufacturing plant capable of producing at least two billion tablets and capsules annually for the treatment of non-communicable diseases.
Established in 2021, AfSNET provides a platform for African states, provinces, counties, municipalities and other sub-sovereign authorities to showcase investment opportunities, engage investors and financiers, improve project development capabilities and contribute to intra-African trade, industrialisation and the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area.
Cross River Secures $20m Oil Palm Investment
Meanwhile, the Cross River State Government has signed a concession agreement with ValueFronteira Limited for the development of a 4,000-hectare oil palm plantation in Ijiegu Yache and adjoining clans in Yala Local Government Area, with the company committing more than $20 million to the project over five years.
The project is expected to create thousands of jobs and boost agricultural production in six clans: Ijiegu, Wonye, Uchu, Ichui, Ukani and Ewor. It forms part of the state government’s agricultural transformation agenda aimed at strengthening food security, promoting rural development and improving livelihoods.
Speaking at a stakeholders’ meeting and site handover ceremony in Ijiegu Yache, the Managing Director of ValueFronteira Limited, Maurice Ekpong, said the company would invest more than $20 million over five years to establish the plantation.
He said the project would generate thousands of employment opportunities and significantly transform the economies of the host communities and the state.
Traditional rulers, community representatives, youths and women leaders welcomed the investment, expressing optimism that it would create jobs, particularly for young people, and stimulate economic activities across the communities.
The Clan Head of Wonye, HRH Mohie Damian Ododo, described the project as a dream come true and pledged the collective support of the clan heads for its successful implementation. He also affirmed ValueFronteira as a corporate member of Yache land.
Other traditional rulers and representatives at the event included HRH Mohie Isaac Omaji, Clan Head of Ijiegu; HRH Mohie Innocent Okaiiba Aji, Clan Head of Ichui; HRH Mohie Ogar Idazor, Clan Head of Ukani; H.H. Augustine Obozor, representing Ewor Clan; and H.H. Pius Idagu, representing Uchu Clan.
In his remarks, the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor and Director-General of the Bureau of Public Private Partnerships, Dr Francis Ntamu, said the concession process was transparent and competitive, leading to ValueFronteira’s emergence as the preferred investor.
He disclosed that the project had received the full approval of the State Executive Council, adding that it aligned with the government’s drive to attract investment and strengthen critical sectors of the economy.
Ntamu said the state government expected the investment to help position Cross River as a major agribusiness destination in Nigeria while advancing food security, rural development and economic empowerment.
“The development is expected to expand commercial agricultural activities in Yala, create employment opportunities and stimulate economic growth in the host communities,” he said.
The government delegation also included the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Solicitor-General of the state, Rosemary Onah, and Brian Ugbe, a director in the Ministry of Agriculture, who represented the Commissioner for Agriculture.

articles.title: DFDS Launches Second Vessel on Italy–Egypt Ro-Ro Route - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: DFDS Launches Second Vessel on Italy–Egypt Ro-Ro Route  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Danish shipping and logistics company DFDS deployed a second vessel on its regular roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) service linking the Italian port of Trieste with Damietta in Egypt, expanding capacity on the route following strong demand since its launch in November 2024.
The inaugural voyage of the second vessel, Ark Futura, was marked by a ceremony on board attended by Captain Søren B. Løvenstein, according to a report issued by the company.
The expansion is expected to strengthen maritime trade links between Egypt and Italy, improve the movement of agricultural products and provide businesses with additional transport capacity between the two Mediterranean markets.
Strong Cargo Performance Drives Expansion
Marco Consalvo, president of the Port Authority of Trieste, said the decision to double the service’s sailing frequency less than two years after its launch reflected strong performance on the route.
He noted that the first vessel had sailed fully loaded in both directions, while the port’s fruit and vegetable sector recorded 31% growth in the first half of the year.
The figures point to growing demand for transport services connecting Egypt with European markets, particularly for time-sensitive agricultural cargo.
Consalvo also highlighted the potential of the Egyptian market, saying that the route through Damietta provides Italian companies with direct access to Egypt and onward commercial opportunities in the Middle East and Gulf region.
Trieste Strengthens Its Role as a European Logistics Hub
Consalvo said Trieste had strengthened its position as a strategic logistics hub for Central and Eastern Europe, supported by its rail network connecting the port with major continental markets within a matter of days.
He added that expanding links with North Africa was becoming increasingly important as companies reorganise supply chains and seek to reduce transport distances.
The port authority chief thanked DFDS and the Samer Group for selecting Trieste and continuing to invest in the service.
The additional vessel is intended to build on the route’s existing commercial performance while strengthening connections between Mediterranean ports and inland European distribution networks.
Egypt–Italy Ro-Ro Route Launched in November 2024
Egypt and Italy launched their Ro-Ro maritime service in November 2024 as part of efforts to establish a more direct transport corridor between Damietta and Trieste.
At the time, Egypt’s Transport Minister, Lieutenant General Kamel El-Wazir, described the project as an important economic initiative designed to strengthen maritime connectivity and establish a green transport corridor between the two countries.
Ro-Ro services allow wheeled cargo, including trucks and trailers, to be driven directly on and off vessels. The route is designed to facilitate the movement of agricultural produce between Egypt and Italy, offering an alternative to conventional freight arrangements.
Egypt introduced incentives to support the service’s commercial viability, including an 88% reduction in port fees, subject to the principle of reciprocal treatment, as well as reductions in road transit charges.
The two countries also signed a series of legal and administrative documents to facilitate operations, covering port cooperation, customs cooperation, international transport and road freight services.
New Capacity Could Support Agricultural Trade
The addition of a second vessel marks a further step in the development of the maritime corridor, with potential benefits for exporters, importers and logistics operators on both sides of the Mediterranean.
For Egyptian agricultural exporters, the service offers a direct maritime connection to Italy and access to onward distribution networks across Europe. Italian businesses, meanwhile, gain an additional link to the Egyptian market and regional trading routes.
The expansion also comes as companies seek more resilient supply chains and transport options that can reduce transit complexity and improve connections between maritime and inland logistics networks.
The route’s future growth will depend on sustained cargo demand, operational reliability and the ability of both ports to support increasing trade volumes.
With DFDS deploying a second vessel, the Damietta–Trieste service is entering a new phase of development, reinforcing its role as a transport link between Egypt, Italy and wider regional markets.

articles.title: Ghana to host UN convention signing on digital cargo documents on October 26 - MyJoyOnline
articles.summary: Ghana to host UN convention signing on digital cargo documents on October 26  MyJoyOnline
articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
Ghana is set to host the signing ceremony for the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents on October 26, 2026, in a move expected to support the digitalisation of trade documentation and improve the efficiency of cross-border transactions.
Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Shippers’ Authority (GSA), Professor Ransford Gyampo, says the Convention will establish a harmonised legal framework for electronic negotiable cargo documents, helping address delays, administrative costs and fraud risks associated with paper-based trade documentation.
Speaking at a media engagement in Accra on October 15, 2026, ahead of the signing ceremony, Professor Gyampo said the initiative would provide the legal foundation for electronic documents to perform the functions of their paper-based equivalents, subject to the Convention’s requirements.
“The continued dependence on paper documents can create delays, increase administrative costs, expose transactions to fraud and complicate the movement of goods across borders,” he said.
Negotiable cargo documents, including bills of lading, play an important role in international commerce by facilitating cargo movement, supporting commercial transactions and providing a basis for trade finance.
The Convention is expected to create opportunities to reduce documentation-related delays, improve transaction efficiency and facilitate access to trade finance, while supporting more integrated digital supply chains.
Professor Gyampo stressed that the initiative goes beyond replacing paper documents with electronic records, arguing that legal certainty and confidence are essential to the digital transformation of international trade.
“The Convention is therefore not simply about replacing paper with electronic records. It is about building the legal certainty and confidence necessary for businesses and institutions to conduct trade in an increasingly digital environment,” he said.
For Ghana, hosting the signing ceremony presents an opportunity to demonstrate its commitment to trade facilitation, digital transformation and stronger regional and international trade connectivity.
Professor Gyampo said the development also aligns with Ghana’s ambition to strengthen its position as a preferred trade and logistics hub in West Africa and advance the objectives of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The Convention is considered particularly relevant to African trade, where cross-border transactions often involve multiple jurisdictions, transport modes and border procedures.
According to Professor Gyampo, a reliable legal framework for electronic negotiable cargo documents could help reduce documentary barriers, improve the flow of trade-related information and support more efficient cargo movement across supply chains.
For Ghanaian importers and exporters, the expected benefits include lower administrative burdens, faster processing of trade transactions, improved opportunities for trade financing and greater predictability in international commerce.
However, Professor Gyampo cautioned that the benefits would depend on sustained efforts beyond the signing ceremony, including the Convention’s adoption, ratification and implementation, as well as the preparedness of businesses, financial institutions, transport operators and regulators to use electronic negotiable cargo documents.
“These benefits will not arise from the signing ceremony alone,” he said, calling for continued stakeholder engagement and the necessary legal, institutional, technological and commercial measures to translate the Convention’s provisions into practical outcomes.
The GSA also called on the media to help raise public awareness of the Convention and explain its implications for trade competitiveness, access to finance and the digitalisation of commercial processes.
The Authority reaffirmed its commitment to working with relevant ministries, the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), industry stakeholders and international partners to promote awareness and support the Convention’s effective adoption and implementation.
Professor Gyampo said modern, predictable and efficient trade documentation was essential to reducing avoidable costs and strengthening the competitiveness of Ghanaian businesses.
The October 26 signing ceremony is expected to bring representatives of governments, international organisations and the global trading community to Accra. The GSA says the event should serve as a starting point for sustained efforts to establish a more efficient, secure and digitally enabled trading environment.

articles.title: Abdessamad Kayouh Keeps His Seat as Morocco’s Transport Minister - Morocco World News
articles.summary: Abdessamad Kayouh Keeps His Seat as Morocco’s Transport Minister  Morocco World News
articles.full_text:
Casablanca – Abdessamad Kayouh will remain Morocco’s Minister of Transport and Logistics after King Mohammed VI appointed the members of the new government at the Royal Palace in Rabat today.
His reappointment keeps the Istiqlal Party politician in charge of a portfolio covering road, rail, maritime and air transport, as well as the country’s logistics infrastructure.
Kayouh first took over the ministry in October 2024, replacing Mohammed Abdeljalil. Before that appointment, he had spent decades in parliamentary politics and the private sector, with a career rooted in the Souss-Massa region.
A Political Career Rooted in Souss
Born on April 11, 1966, in Oulad Teima, in the province of Taroudant, Kayouh grew up in a family with strong ties to agriculture, business, and politics. His father, Haj Ali Kayouh, was a prominent political figure in the Souss region and served as a member of parliament for several decades.
Kayouh studied international trade in Casablanca, graduating in 1988, according to media reports. He later received training in agricultural management in South Africa. His professional career began in the private sector, where he joined the family business and became the general manager of an agricultural company in 1992. The company specialized in producing and exporting citrus fruits and table grapes.
His entry into politics followed in 1997, when he was elected to parliament representing his home region. He won subsequent parliamentary mandates in 2002, 2007 and 2011, building a political base in Taroudant and the wider Souss-Massa area.
He also served as president of the Taroudant provincial council from 2003 to 2009 and held local and regional responsibilities, including positions within the regional council and Oulad Teima municipality.
Kayouh became a member of the Istiqlal Party’s executive committee in 2009. His first ministerial appointment came on January 3, 2012, when King Mohammed VI named him Minister of Handicrafts in the government led by Abdelilah Benkirane. He held the position until July 2013, when Istiqlal’s ministers resigned following the party’s decision to leave the governing coalition.
He later returned to senior parliamentary responsibilities. In 2018, he was elected first vice-president of the House of Councillors, the upper chamber of parliament, and continued to hold a prominent position within Istiqlal.
His appointment as transport minister in October 2024 brought him back to the executive after more than a decade away from a ministerial post.
Transport infrastructure and the 2030 deadline
Kayouh’s current portfolio places him at the center of Morocco’s plans to expand its transport network ahead of the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which the country will co-host with Spain and Portugal. Rail investment is among the major projects on his agenda.
Earlier this month, the minister announced a railway investment program worth MAD 134 billion through 2030. The plan includes extending the high-speed rail line from Kenitra to Marrakech, connecting the future Nador West Med port to the railway network, expanding suburban train services in major urban areas, and acquiring 168 new trains.
The program forms part of broader efforts to modernize the railway network and improve connections between major cities, ports and economic centers. The ministry has also stressed the need for coordinated planning, compatible technical standards and financing arrangements capable of supporting large infrastructure projects.
Read also: Morocco Allocates $13 Billion to Railway Development by 2030
Beyond railways, Kayouh has addressed maritime transport and international logistics. At the first National Maritime Conference in Tangier in May, he pointed to Morocco’s geographic position, port infrastructure and logistics expertise as factors supporting a maritime strategy connecting Europe, Africa and the Atlantic.
He referred to ports including Tanger Med, Nador West Med and the planned Dakhla Atlantique port, alongside links intended to improve access to Atlantic trade routes for Sahel countries.
His ministry has also dealt with practical obstacles facing Moroccan transport companies abroad. At the Logismed trade fair in Casablanca in May, Kayouh said Morocco and the European Union were discussing ways to ease visa procedures for Moroccan professional drivers and international transport operators.
Passenger transport remains another recurring responsibility. During the evaluation of the 2025 Marhaba operation, Kayouh reported that more than 3.2 million passengers and nearly 739,000 vehicles had passed through Moroccan ports between June 10 and September 15.
The operation relied on 13 maritime routes linking Moroccan ports with destinations in Europe, with passenger numbers increasing by 7% compared with 2024.

articles.title: Galamsey turning Ghana’s rivers into ‘chocolate milk’ – Sir Sam Jonah - MyJoyOnline
articles.summary: Galamsey turning Ghana’s rivers into ‘chocolate milk’ – Sir Sam Jonah  MyJoyOnline
articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
The Chancellor of the University of Cape Coast, Sir Sam Jonah, has condemned the devastating impact of illegal mining on Ghana’s environment, warning that the destruction of rivers, forests and farmland makes it impossible to achieve meaningful sustainability.
Speaking at the 25th anniversary conference of Methodist University, he described the pollution of water bodies through illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, as not only an environmental crisis but also an economic, public health and moral concern.
“Rivers that fed our young parents now have the colour of chocolate milk,” he said, illustrating the extent of the destruction caused by the practice.
“This is not only an environmental problem. It is an economic problem. A health problem. And in the end, it is also a moral problem.”
Sir Sam Jonah argued that galamsey reflects a failure of stewardship, with individuals pursuing financial gain at the expense of the environment and the welfare of future generations.
He stressed that sustainability in Ghana must begin with confronting illegal mining and protecting the country's natural resources.
Africa must avoid repeating gold trade mistakes with AI
Beyond environmental concerns, the business mogul warned that Africa risks repeating its historical mistakes in the gold trade as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the global economy.
Drawing on his experience in the mining industry, where he began his career working underground, he said the continent could once again find itself supplying raw resources to others while importing finished products at a higher cost.
He cautioned that Africa could become dependent on foreign AI technologies while exporting its data and paying to access tools developed elsewhere.
“There is a real danger that Africa becomes only a consumer of these technologies and never a creator. That we buy the tools, export our data, pay rent on both,” he said.
“We did that with gold for a century. I pray we don't do this again.”
Sir Sam Jonah urged African countries to invest in developing their own technologies and building the capacity to create solutions suited to their needs, rather than relying primarily on imported innovations.
Mobile money proof of African innovation
He cited mobile money as evidence that Africa has the capacity to develop successful, home-grown solutions when innovators focus on problems affecting local communities.
“Mobile money didn't come from Swiss banks. It grew here because millions of Africans had phones but no bank accounts. And somebody solved that problem. That is African innovation,” he said.
He encouraged entrepreneurs, researchers and policymakers to apply the same approach to sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, logistics and finance, where locally developed technologies could address pressing challenges.
He said the continent must move beyond being a market for imported solutions and become a creator of products, services and technologies that generate economic value.
He also called for a shift from an economy dominated by job seekers to one that produces more entrepreneurs and employment opportunities.
“A nation of job seekers cannot survive. We need a nation of job creators,” he said.
Integrity must guide enterprise and sustainability
Sir Sam Jonah anchored his message on the principles outlined in John Wesley's 1744 sermon, The Use of Money: “Earn all you can, Save all you can, Give all you can.”
He explained that earning should be driven by enterprise and innovation, saving should reflect sustainability, while giving should involve creating opportunities for others.
However, he warned that these principles would lose their value without integrity.
“Without integrity, gaining becomes greed, saving becomes hoarding, and giving becomes patronage,” he said.
He further emphasised the importance of trust in leadership, business and institutional development, noting that it takes considerable time to establish but can be destroyed quickly.
“Trust takes a decade to build and an afternoon to destroy,” he said.
Universities urged to prioritise digital literacy and job creation
The UCC Chancellor also challenged universities to prepare students for an economy increasingly shaped by digital technologies and innovation.
He called for digital literacy to become compulsory for all students, irrespective of their disciplines, including nursing, accounting and theology.
He also urged universities to ensure that research translates into practical solutions that benefit society, rather than remaining confined to academic publications and institutional shelves.
According to him, higher education institutions should measure their success not only by the buildings they construct but also by the businesses their graduates establish and the jobs they create.

articles.title: US Project Vault readies $1B loan blitz for industry - Mining.com
articles.summary: US Project Vault readies $1B loan blitz for industry  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
The US government-backed Project Vault is preparing to issue up to $1 billion in loans to American manufacturers seeking critical minerals, advancing Washington’s efforts to shield domestic industry from supply disruptions.
VaultCo, the entity managing the stockpiling initiative, is in discussions with more than 70 companies across the critical minerals supply chain, Bloomberg reported. The first round of financing is expected to cover more than a dozen original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), with another group to follow.
“What’s likely to happen is we’ll announce several hundred million dollars, maybe a billion dollars, of loans to OEMs who have requested use of the Vault facility,” VaultCo Executive Chairman Brett Lambert told the news outlet. “In the first tranche, we’ll have more than a dozen firms, followed by more than a dozen shortly after.”
The financing would mark a significant step towards making Project Vault operational as the US seeks to reduce its exposure to volatile critical minerals markets and strengthen manufacturers’ access to materials essential for industrial production.
Lambert said the recipients would not be publicly identified at this stage, although the announcement is expected to disclose the types of minerals they have requested.
Stockpile takes shape
Launched in February, Project Vault is structured as an independently governed public-private partnership backed by a $10 billion loan from the US Export-Import Bank (EXIM) and nearly $2 billion in private investment.
Commodity trading giants Glencore (LON: GLEN) and Mercuria recently committed $500 million each, becoming the first commodity traders to join the initiative.
Mercuria has already delivered 12,000 tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo, establishing a new destination for the African country’s metal within Washington’s supply security strategy.
The shipment comes amid growing US demand for Congolese copper. Imports reached a record 53,290 tonnes in July, driven by competitive prices, improved product quality and concerns over potential tariffs that prompted buyers to accelerate shipments.
Commercial imports and Project Vault serve different purposes. While conventional purchases meet immediate industrial demand, the reserve is intended to provide manufacturers with access to materials when normal supply channels become disrupted.
Tailored mineral demand
Unlike conventional government stockpiles, Project Vault is designed around manufacturers’ specific requirements rather than predetermined inventories of strategic commodities.
Participating companies have requested not only raw metals and minerals but also specialized magnets, powders, alloys and other processed materials tailored to their production needs.
“There isn’t any one mineral that stands out, but the specificity of the requests have surprised me,” Lambert told Bloomberg.
The demand-driven approach allows manufacturers to determine which materials are purchased and stored, potentially giving smaller buyers greater purchasing power in fragmented and often opaque markets.
It also distinguishes Project Vault from the US National Defense Stockpile, which the Defense Logistics Agency administers to secure materials required for national defence.
The next test will be whether the initial loans can translate manufacturers’ highly specific requests into reliable inventories, particularly for processed materials that may be harder to source than raw commodities.

articles.title: Investing in regional transport corridors key to ensure long-term expansion of logistics - Namibia Economist
articles.summary: Investing in regional transport corridors key to ensure long-term expansion of logistics  Namibia Economist

By Hosea Shishiveni. *
Namibia stands at a critical crossroads in the future of regional transport and logistics. For years, the Port of Walvis Bay and its transport corridors have offered landlocked countries in southern Africa an alternative gateway to international markets. However, the growing investment in Angola’s Lobito Corridor is changing the competitive landscape, particularly for the movement of copper, cobalt and other goods from Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
At the same time, Namibia and Botswana are advancing discussions on the proposed Trans-Kalahari Railway, an initiative that could strengthen regional connectivity and open new economic opportunities. The challenge is therefore not simply to choose one corridor over another, but to determine how Namibia can protect its existing markets, attract new cargo and remain a competitive regional logistics hub.
The Lobito Corridor links Angola’s Atlantic Port of Lobito with the mineral-rich regions of the DRC through the Benguela railway. Its strategic importance lies in its ability to transport minerals from inland production centres to international markets through an Atlantic port. The corridor is attracting increasing political and financial support, with infrastructure investments intended to improve railway capacity and strengthen connections between Angola, Zambia and the DRC.
The proposed Zambia–Lobito railway is particularly significant because it is intended to establish a more direct rail connection between Zambia’s Copperbelt and Angola. Although this proposed connection is still subject to development and implementation milestones, its potential impact on regional freight movements should not be underestimated.
For Namibia, these developments should serve as a strategic warning. Zambia and the DRC are not permanently tied to a single transport route. If the Lobito Corridor offers competitive tariffs, reliable railway services, efficient border procedures and attractive transit times, businesses will have commercial reasons to use it. Namibia should therefore not wait until significant cargo has shifted elsewhere before responding. Regional logistics competitiveness is increasingly determined by the quality of infrastructure, the cost of transportation, the reliability of delivery schedules and the ability of governments to provide efficient cross-border services.
The Walvis Bay–Ndola–Lubumbashi Development Corridor (WBNLDC) remains one of Namibia’s most important regional economic assets. Connecting Walvis Bay through northern Namibia to Zambia and the southern DRC, the corridor provides landlocked economies with access to international markets through Namibia’s Atlantic port. Its importance extends beyond the movement of goods, as it supports not only trucking companies but also clearing agents, warehouses, fuel suppliers, maintenance workshops, accommodation establishments and numerous small businesses along the route. It also creates opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship in towns and communities connected to the transport network. However, much of this economic potential depends on the efficiency of road transport, border crossings, cargo handling and connections between different modes of transportation.
Namibia must therefore confront an important question: if regional competitors are investing in railway infrastructure while the WBNLDC remains heavily dependent on road freight, how will the corridor remain competitive when customers increasingly demand lower transportation costs, reliable delivery schedules and efficient bulk freight services? Road transport will continue to play an important role, but the government should examine whether strategically targeted railway investment could reduce the cost of moving certain categories of cargo. A comprehensive review of the corridor should identify infrastructure gaps, assess customer demand and determine which improvements would provide the greatest economic returns.
One proposal deserving serious consideration is the development of a railway connection extending from Grootfontein to Katima Mulilo, integrated with Namibia’s existing railway network and where commercially and technically feasible, connected to the wider regional railway system.
Grootfontein occupies a strategic position in northern Namibia’s transport network while Katima Mulilo provides an important road connection to Zambia. Strengthening the logistics links between these locations could improve cargo consolidation, support intermodal transportation and create new opportunities for regional trade. Nevertheless, such a railway should not be built simply because it appears strategically attractive. It would require a rigorous feasibility study examining construction costs, projected freight volumes, railway gauge compatibility, border infrastructure, operating expenses and the expected return on investment. The study should also compare the proposal with alternatives such as upgrading existing railway infrastructure, improving roads and establishing intermodal freight terminals.
Alongside railway development, Namibia should further investigate the establishment of dry ports and logistics centres in Grootfontein and Katima Mulilo. Properly planned facilities could provide warehousing, cargo handling, container management, customs-related services and distribution facilities for businesses serving northern Namibia, Zambia and neighbouring markets. Such investments could reduce delays, encourage freight consolidation and attract private-sector investment. However, dry ports must be supported by reliable electricity, water, digital connectivity, good road infrastructure and effective customs coordination. They must also be commercially viable, with sufficient cargo volumes to justify their establishment and operation. If implemented strategically, these facilities could help transform the corridor from a route through which goods merely pass into an economic network that creates employment and business opportunities for local communities.
The proposed Trans-Kalahari Railway between Botswana and Walvis Bay presents another important opportunity for Namibia. The project is intended to strengthen Botswana’s access to the Atlantic Ocean and could increase the movement of bulk commodities through Namibia. It could also support investment in port services, railway operations, engineering and logistics management.
However, Namibia must distinguish between the markets served by the different corridors. The Trans-Kalahari Railway is principally associated with connecting Botswana’s inland production centres, for instance its coal-producing areas, with Walvis Bay, while the WBNLDC is strategically important for trade with Zambia and the DRC. Although there may be opportunities for the corridors to complement one another, they serve different commercial purposes and should not be treated as interchangeable projects.
The Trans-Kalahari Railway should therefore not become a distraction from the urgent need to protect and strengthen the WBNLDC. Instead, both initiatives should form part of an integrated national transport and logistics strategy. Namibia should pursue investments that diversify cargo sources, strengthen regional trade and reduce dependence on any single commodity or market. The government must also ensure that public resources are allocated according to commercial viability, projected demand and measurable economic benefits. Infrastructure projects should be evaluated according to their ability to improve freight efficiency, create sustainable employment and strengthen Namibia’s competitiveness over the long term.
Namibia needs a forward-looking transport strategy that recognises the growing competition between regional logistics networks. The Ministry of Works and Transport should work with Namport, TransNamib, the Walvis Bay Corridor Group, the Namibia Revenue Agency, regional authorities and private sector stakeholders to develop a coordinated investment plan. This plan should compare the commercial performance of the WBNLDC, the Lobito Corridor and the proposed Trans-Kalahari Railway, taking into account freight demand, transit times, tariffs, infrastructure costs and long-term economic benefits. Namibia should also strengthen digital customs systems, improve border coordination, expand cargo-handling capacity and encourage private investment in warehousing and distribution. These improvements could strengthen the competitiveness of Walvis Bay even before major railway projects are completed.
Furthermore, corridor development must deliver tangible benefits to the communities through which these transport routes pass. Young people and small businesses in Grootfontein, Katima Mulilo and other towns along the corridor should benefit through technical training, employment, transport services and opportunities to supply larger logistics operators. Local businesses should be encouraged to participate in warehousing, vehicle maintenance, catering, accommodation, security and other services associated with the movement of goods. A transport corridor should not merely move minerals and consumer products across Namibia; it should create opportunities for local economic development and contribute to national prosperity.
The Lobito Corridor demonstrates that regional logistics leadership cannot be taken for granted. The Trans-Kalahari Railway offers Namibia an additional opportunity to strengthen its position, but it must be pursued alongside, rather than instead of, the strategic development of the Walvis Bay–Ndola–Lubumbashi Development Corridor. Namibia should not view these transport routes as competing political projects. They are instruments of national development whose value depends on sound planning, commercial viability, regional cooperation and effective implementation.

In 2024, South Africa and Nepal marked 30 years of formal diplomatic relations. Yet, the ties between the two countries stretch back well beyond the establishment of official diplomatic channels in 1994. Nepal played a significant role in South Africa’s struggle against apartheid, serving as vice-chair of the United Nations Special Committee against Apartheid for 25 years. This legacy of solidarity continues to underpin bilateral relations, which are shaped by shared democratic values, engagement through the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), a commitment to UN peacekeeping and common advocacy for climate action and greater representation of the Global South.
Based at the High Commission of South Africa in New Delhi, which also represents South Africa in Nepal and Bangladesh on a non-resident basis, High Commissioner H.E. Prof. Anil Sooklal oversees bilateral engagement across the region. Following visits by South African officials in 2012 and 2015, the two countries held their first bilateral consultations in Pretoria in March 2022. Since then, they have sought to translate diplomatic goodwill into practical coopeforation. The Declaration of Intent signed in 2022 provides a framework for expanding economic diplomacy, promoting trade and investment, and strengthening technical cooperation.
Despite longstanding political ties and shared interests in adventure tourism, bilateral trade remains limited. However, opportunities for deeper engagement are emerging in areas such as mineral exploration, civil aviation training, agro-processing, information and communication technology, and city-to-city cooperation between Kathmandu and Cape Town.
Speaking to Onlinekhabar, High Commissioner Sooklal discusses the historical ties between South Africa and Nepal, the prospects for trade, investment and educational cooperation, and the potential for both countries to advance shared priorities through multilateral platforms, including BRICS and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
Welcome to Nepal, Your Excellency. What is your purpose for this visit?
Well, as you know, I am accredited as the High Commissioner of South Africa to Nepal. So, from time to time, I come here to see how we can strengthen our relationship—not only at the government level, but also within the business sector, civil society, academia, and think tanks.
We have had a very productive past four days in Kathmandu. You have a new government in place, so it was important for us to come and introduce ourselves and explore how we can continue working with this new administration. We follow developments in Nepal very closely.
We sent condolences from our president and the people of South Africa pertaining to the tragic events of August 26. As you know, there were six South Africans who were part of a visit to Nepal and were impacted by the flash floods; they are still missing. As High Commissioner, I am constantly getting requests for updates—not just from the families, but because this tragedy and its impact have been widely reported in South Africa. We want to reiterate our condolences and our solidarity with the government and people of Nepal.
During the past few days, we had the pleasure of meeting the Foreign Secretary, who is a good friend of mine because he previously served in South Africa as the High Commissioner of Nepal, and I knew him from that time. We discussed strengthening cooperation with the Foreign Ministry, and we also had a very productive meeting with the Foreign Minister, Shishir Khanal. We have invited him to South Africa to see how we can further strengthen relations between our two countries.
Now, not many people are aware that Nepal played a very important role in our freedom struggle. As you know, in 1962, the UN created the Special Committee Against Apartheid, and Nepal served on that committee. From 1969 until our democracy in 1994—when that committee was disbanded—Nepal served as the vice-chair for 25 years. So, Nepal was a very important part of the UN system in championing our freedom and democracy.
President Nelson Mandela spoke about this when he was released from prison, sending a message of appreciation for the vital role Nepal played within the international system during our freedom struggle. We share a historical relationship. We formed formal diplomatic ties in 1994, and our political relations are very strong because we cooperate closely on multilateral platforms within the UN. We are both vibrant democracies that believe in multilateralism and the UN system.
Furthermore, both of us champion issues of climate action, which is critical. The melting of the Himalayan glaciers and the impact it is having on your country is not of Nepal’s making—Nepal’s global carbon footprint is negligible, yet you are bearing the brunt of global warming. I think it is important that we continue to work within the UNFCCC to champion climate action, especially technology sharing to address both mitigation and adaptation.
Equally important is cooperating on disaster risk reduction. Global warming is causing sea levels to rise, and climate change is impacting countries across the world. The flash flooding we are seeing has a direct impact not only on human lives, but also on food security and other dimensions of our existence. These are some of the discussions we have had regarding how we can strengthen cooperation at both bilateral and multilateral levels, given that we are largely on the same page on these issues. We are very positive about the meetings we had with the Foreign Ministry and how we can take this relationship forward.
You celebrated 30 years of diplomatic relations in 2024, yet bilateral trade and investment remain very modest. Why has the economic relationship not grown more substantially?
I think the major factor is that despite having historical ties and very strong government-to-government relations, at the people-to-people level—including the private sector—we simply don’t know enough about each other. This is one of the things I have been highlighting: we need to exchange trade missions and identify three or four key areas for mutual benefit.
During this visit—both in my meeting with the Minister of Industry and Commerce and with the Nepal Chamber of Commerce—we identified several critical sectors. First is mining and minerals, as South Africa is a major mining nation and Nepal has vast mineral deposits that have yet to be fully explored. South Africa has extensive experience in this area, including critical minerals essential for green technologies. Second is infrastructure and ICT.
Given recent devastation, there are major infrastructure needs for reconstruction and general advancement. Nepal has a young, well-educated population skilled in new technologies, while Cape Town is becoming the African capital for data processing, BPO, and new technologies, presenting a strong partnership opportunity. Third is agro-processing, where South Africa is quite advanced. Finally, tourism offers vast opportunities, as travellers seek out Mount Everest and Nepal’s nature just as Cape Town remains a hugely popular destination.
To translate these into practical steps, we agreed with the Nepal Chamber of Commerce to twin their Women in Business wing with the South African BRICS Women’s Alliance, focusing on mainstreaming women and youth into the MSME sector. We also agreed to explore twinning the Nepal Chamber of Commerce with the South African Chamber of Commerce and Industry, alongside facilitating reciprocal trade delegations.
On the people-to-people and institutional front, what other initiatives are underway?
We had two very good meetings regarding local and community ties. For city twinning, we met with the Mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City and are exploring the possibility of twinning Kathmandu with Cape Town, creating a natural top-to-tip synergy between Kathmandu near Mount Everest and Cape Town at the southern tip of Africa. Regarding civic organisations, I met with the Rotary Club of Kathmandu and have already made contact with the Rotary Club of Cape Town to explore twinning the two chapters, given their shared focus on social upliftment and community development.
For think tanks and academia, we met with the Ambassadors’ Club to strengthen cooperation between South African research institutes and Nepalese think tanks, paving the way for student and academic exchanges. Lastly, regarding journalist exchanges, we want to restart the program that previously brought Nepali journalists to South Africa to give our bilateral relationship greater public visibility.
The two countries signed a Declaration of Intent on cooperation in 2022, focusing on trade, investment, tourism, education, and people-to-people ties. What concrete steps will turn this into reality?
As I mentioned, we must move from good discussions to practical implementation. We have agreed on initiating reciprocal trade delegation exchanges starting next year, alongside fast-tracking the twinning of our Rotary clubs and the cities of Kathmandu and Cape Town.
We are also exploring academic pathways. South African universities have some of the oldest and most respected faculties in mineralogy and mining studies—such as the University of the Witwatersrand, the University of Pretoria, and the University of Cape Town. Tuition in South Africa is a fraction of the cost compared to Europe or Australia, and many universities offer full scholarships for foreign students.
Additionally, we plan to invite the Council for Geoscience in South Africa—a state entity that has assisted countries like India with mineral mapping—to help Nepal identify and map its mineral deposits.
