articles.full_text:
BRICS is prioritising payment interoperability and local-currency trade over a common currency, pursuing financial integration without monetary union or displacing the dollar’s structural dominance
Image Source:  Getty Images 
The BRICS grouping convened in New Delhi and, for the thirteenth consecutive year, did not establish a common currency. Instead, the bloc advanced work on linking national payment systems, not creating a new currency to rival the dollar — a development that may prove more consequential.
The proposal for a common BRICS currency has surfaced repeatedly at successive summits but has yet to materialise. The 2026 summit was convened at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on 12 and 13 September, with no common-currency proposal emerging. Less widely covered, but arguably more important in practical terms, was the Payment Task Force’s renewed mandate to pursue interoperability among the national payment systems of the bloc’s 11 members. This infrastructural dimension of BRICS cooperation has received less scholarly and policy attention than it warrants as the bloc’s most tangible area of institutional progress.
The New Delhi declaration, issued at the conclusion of the eighteenth BRICS summit under India’s chairship, directed officials to continue work on efficient cross-border payment mechanisms, examine interoperability between payment and messaging systems, and advance trade settlement in members’ respective national currencies. It did not call for the development of a common currency.
This position was corroborated by statements from India’s Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra around the time of the summit. Both confirmed that a BRICS currency remained outside the bloc’s active agenda.
This is not a recent shift. Brazil’s BRICS sherpa, Mauricio Lyrio, articulated a similar position in 2025, identifying the bloc’s practical priority as reducing the cost of trade and financial transactions through greater use of national currencies rather than creating a new one. Despite recurring commentary to the contrary, this position has remained consistent.
The issue also merits consideration within a longer institutional history. The proposal for a common currency first emerged publicly around the 2013 Durban summit, where it was discussed alongside plans that subsequently led to the establishment of the New Development Bank (NDB).
The summit ultimately produced the bank, not a common currency. The distinction is institutionally important: a development bank that provides project financing operates on fundamentally different terms from a central bank responsible for issuing currency, managing the money supply and acting as a lender of last resort during periods of financial instability.
This distinction remains as relevant today as it was thirteen years ago. Establishing a common currency would require BRICS member states — which differ substantially in their inflation histories, capital-control regimes and strategic priorities — to agree on currency issuance, coordinated monetary policy, reserve management and mechanisms for addressing economic divergence.
No member state has indicated a willingness to cede this degree of monetary sovereignty, and such a development appears unlikely in the foreseeable future. Yet commentary predicting the dollar’s imminent displacement continues to recur around each summit, often independently of the bloc’s documented institutional positions.
The more substantive developments have received considerably less coverage, despite their potentially greater practical significance. Russia operates its Faster Payments System, Mir card network and System for Transfer of Financial Messages (SPFS). India has developed the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), which functions as a core component of its domestic payments infrastructure. Brazil operates Pix, while China has established an extensive renminbi clearing and settlement network centred on the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which is reported to reach approximately 190 countries and regions. Indonesia, a more recent BRICS partner, operates QRIS.
Each system serves its domestic market, but cross-border transactions can encounter additional costs and operational barriers. These systems were not all designed to interoperate directly with one another.
BRICS Pay is intended to address this gap through a proposed mechanism for linking systems such as CIPS, UPI, Pix and SPFS. Its objective is to facilitate settlement in national currencies without requiring routine reliance on the US dollar or the SWIFT messaging system. This represents a more incremental form of de-dollarisation: rather than replacing the dollar with an alternative currency, it seeks to develop payment infrastructure that could reduce the need for dollar intermediation in some transactions.
The New Development Bank has pursued a comparable, lower-profile approach by expanding local-currency financing, which reportedly accounts for approximately one quarter of its approved project financing.
Separately, mBridge, the cross-border central bank digital currency platform developed with the participation of the Bank for International Settlements, had processed cumulative transactions exceeding US$ 55 billion by early 2026, with the substantial majority denominated in digital yuan.
None of these initiatives requires the creation of a shared monetary policy framework. Instead, such initiatives rely on technical standards and operational coordination — undertakings that are generally narrower in scope and less politically sensitive than monetary integration. This helps explain why payment infrastructure may offer a more practical avenue for BRICS cooperation than a common currency.
India’s position within this broader development merits closer analytical attention, given that it holds the bloc’s chairship while explicitly distancing itself from the common-currency proposal often associated with BRICS. The Union Commerce and Industry Minister’s outreach to fellow BRICS members highlighted UPI’s operational scale — processing tens of billions of transactions each month in India — as a potential model for extending payment interoperability across the bloc, rather than developing parallel systems independently.
This position is coherent for a state that has, over the preceding decade, built one of the world’s most extensive public digital payments infrastructures. India has a clear interest in encouraging other members to adopt or connect with its existing infrastructure, rather than develop competing systems from scratch. Acknowledging this strategic interest does not, in itself, undermine the merits of India’s proposal, but it is essential to understanding its position.
Central bank digital currencies introduce a further dimension to this development, and it is at this juncture that the picture becomes substantively more uncertain rather than merely repetitive. All ten BRICS member states are pursuing central bank digital currency initiatives. Nine have reached the pilot stage, while two, Egypt and Ethiopia, remain at the research stage. None has achieved full implementation, and these national pilots do not yet constitute an interoperable network across the bloc.
Reporting on the New Delhi summit indicated that the Reserve Bank of India had proposed linking the digital currencies of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa through shared infrastructure and governance standards, with a particular focus on trade finance and tourism-related payments. Whether this proposal proves durable, given the differences among five regulatory regimes and the prospect of sustained scrutiny from Washington, remains a separate and unresolved question. The United States administration under Donald Trump has characterised the bloc as anti-American and has threatened tariffs against states perceived as aligning with it. This creates a form of external pressure that, in comparable historical instances, has either curtailed such initiatives or accelerated them. The bloc’s institutional history suggests the latter outcome is more likely.
Notwithstanding this level of institutional activity, the dollar's international position has not deteriorated substantially. Its share of global official reserves has declined to below 57 percent, a measurable shift that warrants attention. Yet the dollar continues to account for approximately 88 percent of global foreign exchange turnover. This pattern does not indicate a currency in structural retreat, but rather a currency that continues to perform the substantial majority of its underlying function despite sustained discourse about its decline. The more precise characterisation of the outcome achieved in New Delhi is not de-dollarisation in any structural sense, but a marginal reduction in transactional friction, a development of genuine though understated analytical significance.
A discernible pattern emerges when these initiatives are considered collectively, one that BRICS appears to have adopted, whether through deliberate design or institutional default, as an operating principle: the pursuit of payment cooperation without monetary union, local-currency financing without a shared treasury, and standards harmonisation without a common regulator. This does not constitute a project of transferring sovereignty upwards to a new supranational monetary authority. It resembles instead what the economist Dani Rodrik has characterised, in a related analytical context, as the effort to reconcile national sovereignty with deeper international integration without requiring either full political union or full fragmentation. In this sense, it represents a horizontal connection of sovereign systems rather than their consolidation into a single institutional structure.

Deendayal Port Authority is considering using an oil jetty to load bagged rice as around 70 vessels await berths at Kandla. Alongside immediate operational measures, the authority has submitted a ₹47,000-crore waterfront development proposal, highlighting the need to address both current congestion and longer-term capacity constraints.
Rice exports increase pressure on berths
Deendayal Port congestion has intensified as rice exporters switch from containers to conventional vessels, increasing demand for break-bulk handling.
Chairman Sushil Kumar Singh said higher container freight rates to the Middle East had encouraged the change. Some ships face waits of 20–25 days.
The immediate response includes adapting a liquid-cargo jetty for rice trucks and using barges to load vessels at mooring points. These measures would provide alternatives to conventional dry-cargo berths.
Waterfront proposal follows immediate measures
The authority has proposed developing six kilometres of waterfront outside Kandla Creek in four phases, with an estimated overall investment of ₹47,000 crore.
The first phase, estimated at ₹6,400 crore, would involve a trestle and berth for bulk and break-bulk cargo under an engineering, procurement and construction model.
The proposal has been submitted to the shipping ministry; it represents planned development rather than an approved construction programme.
Congestion changes the economics of cargo movement
The situation illustrates a commercial trade-off for exporters: savings on one part of the transport chain can create additional costs elsewhere.
Moving bagged cargo through conventional ships involves different loading arrangements from containerised transport. Vessel schedules, labour availability, cargo assembly and loading sequences all influence the overall cost.
For cargo owners, the relevant comparison is therefore the complete journey, including inland movement, port handling, vessel waiting and delivery commitments.
A lower freight quotation alone does not establish the cheapest end-to-end option. Equally, a longer wait may remain commercially acceptable where other savings outweigh the additional expense.
The practical challenge is to give exporters dependable choices while improving the flow of cargo through existing facilities.
Earlier connectivity approval addresses the landside
Kandla’s infrastructure programme also includes a separate road connectivity project approved earlier this year.
On April 3, 2026, the government announced approval of ₹132.51 crore for a road overbridge at level crossing LC-235 at Deendayal Port.
Western Railway was undertaking construction on a deposit basis. The project forms part of the Sagarmala programme and aligns with the PM Gati Shakti approach to coordinated infrastructure development.
Its purpose is to remove a road–rail crossing bottleneck and improve the movement of port-bound cargo. Upon completion, the bridge is expected to support faster evacuation and more continuous traffic flows.
This investment addresses a different constraint from vessel berthing. Both matter: additional waterfront handling capacity requires sufficient road and rail access to prevent congestion accumulating elsewhere in the logistics chain.
Tuna-Tekra adds a separate container dimension
Another established development is DP World’s planned mega-container terminal at Tuna-Tekra, near the existing port.
The concession announced in 2023 envisaged annual capacity of 2.19 million TEUs, backed by approximately $510 million in investment.
The terminal design includes a 1,100-metre berth capable of accommodating vessels carrying more than 18,000 TEUs, with provision for further berth extension.
The concession follows a build-operate-transfer structure for 30 years, with an option for another 20 years. The original announcement identified 2027 as the completion year.
Its hinterland connections are intended to serve northern, western and central India through road, rail and dedicated freight corridor networks.
The container terminal is a distinct project from the newly proposed bulk and break-bulk waterfront development. Their different cargo markets and handling requirements are important when assessing how future investment could influence port capacity.
Implementation must connect ships, storage and transport
The immediate test is whether operational changes can release usable capacity without disrupting other cargo streams.
Over the longer term, the quality of planning will matter as much as the scale of investment. Berths, storage, truck circulation and rail evacuation must work together to sustain higher throughput.
For shipping companies and exporters, the most useful outcomes would be shorter and more predictable waiting times, reliable loading schedules and clearer visibility of cargo readiness.
The proposed expansion offers a route towards addressing structural constraints. Its commercial value will ultimately depend on approvals, delivery and how effectively the new facilities connect with the wider supply chain.
FAQs
Why are rice shipments contributing to congestion?
A shift from containers to bagged break-bulk shipments has increased demand for conventional cargo-handling facilities.
What immediate measure is being considered?
Adapting an oil jetty to support rice loading.
Is the ₹47,000-crore expansion approved?
It has been proposed to the ministry; the report does not establish final approval.
What is the planned capacity of the Tuna-Tekra container terminal?
Its announced design capacity is 2.19 million TEUs annually.
How would the road overbridge help?
It is intended to remove a level-crossing bottleneck and improve landside cargo movement.
